Title: The Moral and Economic Imperative of a 100% Land Value Tax: A Georgist Case for Reform

In an era of widening inequality, stagnant wages, housing crises, and inefficient tax systems, a bold yet overlooked solution stands ready to transform society: the full implementation of a 100% Land Value Tax (LVT) on the unimproved value of land, drawing from the foundational principles of Henry George’s economic philosophy. Georgism—a school of thought that attributes economic rent, particularly land rent, as a primary source of societal inequity—offers a radical yet elegant solution to the failures of modern taxation and governance. By capturing 100% of land rent for public benefit and eliminating all other taxes, society can create a just, efficient, and prosperous economy. This essay argues that a full Land Value Tax is not only economically superior but also a moral imperative, ensuring fairness, encouraging productivity, and establishing the land rent as the sole legitimate source of public revenue.

The Nature of Land and the Unearned Increment of Rent

At the heart of Georgist theory is a clear distinction between land and capital. Land—defined as all natural resources, including physical space, mineral rights, water, and airspace—is not created by human effort. Unlike buildings, machinery, or labor, which are products of human toil and enterprise, land exists independently of human action. Its value is not the result of the landowner’s labor, but of community development: infrastructure, population growth, public services, and social investment. A vacant lot in Manhattan is worth millions not because its owner is industrious, but because of the economic activity, transportation, and opportunities created collectively by society.

This unearned income derived from land ownership is known as economic rent—the surplus value captured by landowners due to scarcity and location, without any corresponding productive effort. Henry George argued forcefully in Progress and Poverty (1879) that allowing private individuals to capture this rent is akin to privatizing public wealth. When land values rise due to public investment—say, the construction of a subway station—the beneficiary is often a passive land speculator, not the taxpayers who funded the improvement. This represents not only injustice but a perverse incentive structure that rewards idleness and speculation over productivity.

The Efficiency and Neutrality of a Land Value Tax

One of the most compelling arguments for a 100% LVT is its efficiency. Unlike taxes on income, sales, or capital, a land value tax does not discourage productive activity. Economists across the ideological spectrum, from Adam Smith to Milton Friedman, have recognized that land taxes are among the least distortionary and most efficient forms of taxation.

Because land is fixed in supply—no one can create more of it and its quantity cannot be hidden or moved—a tax on its unimproved value cannot reduce its availability. A higher tax on land does not deter landowners from "producing" more land; it simply recaptures the value that society creates. This makes LVT uniquely neutral: it does not alter incentives to work, save, invest, or build. In fact, it encourages the productive use of land. Under a full LVT, owners are no longer rewarded for holding prime land idle in speculation. If they do not develop it or use it efficiently, they still must pay the full tax on its value—compelling underutilized urban parcels, vacant lots, and land banking practices to give way to housing, commerce, and community use.

Moreover, by eliminating taxes on wages, profits, and sales, a full LVT would dramatically reduce the cost of labor and production. Workers would keep their full earnings. Entrepreneurs could innovate without tax penalties. Consumers would face no sales tax barriers. Businesses would no longer need elaborate tax shelters. The economy would operate with dramatically lower transaction costs and greater fluidity. This shift would unleash unprecedented economic dynamism, fostering innovation and equitable growth.

Fairness and Justice: Recapturing Public Wealth

Fairness is the moral cornerstone of the Georgist argument. The current tax system disproportionately burdens productive citizens while allowing landlords and real estate speculators to profit from unearned gains. Property taxes, as they exist today, often tax improvements (buildings) as heavily as or more heavily than land, penalizing those who improve their property. This perversely encourages blight, disinvestment, and urban decay.

A 100% LVT rectifies this injustice by ensuring that the value created by the community—through collective effort, public investment, and population—flows back to the community. Rather than subsidizing land hoarding and speculative enrichment, it institutionalizes the principle that “value, which is created by the community, belongs to the community.” This is not confiscation but a rightful recapturing of public wealth that was never legitimately private to begin with.

Consider the case of a billionaire who owns thousands of acres of undeveloped land. Under the current system, their tax burden may be minimal relative to the appreciation they gain as infrastructure expands around their holdings. With a 100% LVT, they contribute proportionally to the value they benefit from—no more, no less. They could still keep the land, but only if they are willing to pay the full social rental value it commands. This does not penalize wealth; it ensures that wealth not earned through production or investment is not retained at society’s expense.

Furthermore, a single tax on land rent would drastically simplify the tax code. No more corporate returns, income audits, or complex deductions. The administrative burden on both government and taxpayers would diminish. Compliance would soar because land cannot be hidden offshore or understated with accounting tricks. Transparency would increase, and corruption would decrease.

Environmental Sustainability and Urban Revitalization

Beyond economic efficiency and fairness, a 100% LVT promotes environmental and spatial sustainability. By making land ownership costly in proportion to its value, it discourages urban sprawl and encourages high-density, transit-oriented development. Cities would naturally grow upward, not outward, preserving greenfields and reducing automobile dependency. Mixed-use development would flourish, fostering walkable communities and vibrant public spaces.

Speculative holding of agricultural land and natural ecosystems—often a driver of deforestation, pollution, and biodiversity loss—would decline as owners face pressure to use land productively or sell it to those who will. Conservation might even be incentivized: public or nonprofit entities could acquire ecologically sensitive land, knowing they would pay only for its unimproved value, not for hypothetical development potential. Land for parks, renewable energy, or community farming would become more accessible.

In cities, the LVT would catalyze the redevelopment of slums and derelict areas. Landlords would no longer benefit from leaving buildings to crumble while waiting for land values to rise. The tax would make it financially rational to renovate and invest. Combined with the abolition of other taxes, this would create a powerful one-two punch: lower operating costs for businesses and residents, paired with higher incentives to develop urban land. The result? Affordable housing, reduced congestion, and revitalized neighborhoods.

Addressing Objections

Critics argue that a 100% LVT would be confiscatory or unjust to long-term landowners, particularly homeowners who have built equity over decades. But this concern misunderstands the structure of the tax. A full LVT does not tax homes, improvements, or personal wealth—it taxes only the unimproved value of land. A family homeowner with a modest lot in a suburban neighborhood would pay far less than a developer holding vacant land in downtown Seattle or Manhattan.

Moreover, transitional policies can be implemented to phase in the tax, protect vulnerable populations, and allow for adjustment. For example, landowners could be permitted to defer tax payments (with interest) until the land is sold, preventing forced displacement. Additionally, the abolition of income, payroll, and sales taxes would compensate most citizens with greater disposable income and lower living costs.

Another objection is that land values are subjective and difficult to assess. Yet modern Geographic Information Systems (GIS), automated valuation models, and mass appraisal techniques make accurate land valuation not only possible but increasingly precise. Many countries—including Denmark, Estonia, and Taiwan—have successfully implemented land-based taxation with high accuracy and public acceptance.

Finally, skeptics question whether land rent can generate enough revenue to fund all government services. But empirical evidence suggests otherwise. Economists estimate that land rent constitutes between 20% and 30% of national income in developed economies. In urbanized nations, the figure may be even higher. With intelligent spending and the elimination of tax evasion and inefficiencies inherent in complex tax systems, land rent alone can—and should—be sufficient to finance essential public goods: education, healthcare, infrastructure, and social services.

A Vision for a Just and Prosperous Society

Imagine a society where work is rewarded, not taxed. Where innovation flourishes without regulatory burden. Where housing is abundant and affordable because no one profits from withholding land. Where cities are vibrant, sustainable, and inclusive. Where public wealth circulates back to the public, rather than enriching a rent-seeking elite. This is not utopia—it is the attainable outcome of a single, principled reform: a 100% tax on land value.

Henry George’s insight remains as radical and urgent today as it was in the 19th century: poverty persists not because of scarcity, but because of the monopolization of natural opportunity. A full Land Value Tax is not merely a fiscal tool; it is a restoration of economic justice. It aligns individual incentives with the common good. It treats land not as private plunder, but as a shared inheritance.

Governments should abandon the patchwork of inefficient, inequitable, and counterproductive taxes. They should embrace the simplicity, fairness, and power of capturing land rent for public benefit. The time has come to make land value the sole source of public revenue—not as an experiment, but as a moral and economic necessity.

The solution is not more taxes, but better taxes. And the best tax of all is the one we already pay, invisibly, through rising rents and housing costs: the rent we pay to private landlords for what rightfully belongs to all. It is time to claim it—for justice, for prosperity, and for the future.

A 100% land value tax on the unimproved value of land is not merely a clever tax reform. It is the most just, efficient, and economically sound basis for public finance ever proposed. Rooted in Georgist economic principles, it recognizes a simple but profound truth: land is not produced by human effort, cannot be legitimately monopolized by private claim, and derives its value overwhelmingly from nature, location, and the presence of society itself. Therefore, the rental value of land should belong to everyone equally, and the public should capture it in full for common benefit. Land value is socially created, not privately earned

The central moral insight of Georgism is that while people have a natural right to the fruits of their labor, they do not have a natural right to the mere privilege of excluding others from the earth. Labor creates wealth; land exists prior to and independently of labor. A parcel of urban land becomes valuable not because the owner made it so, but because roads, schools, public safety, nearby workers, commerce, infrastructure, and the surrounding community make that location desirable. A vacant lot in the center of a city can be worth millions even if the owner has done nothing to improve it. That value is not a reward for productive effort. It is a charge created by society.

To allow a private individual to collect this socially generated rent is to permit a transfer from the many to the few. The owner benefits from public development without necessarily contributing to it, while everyone else pays higher rents, higher housing costs, and higher barriers to entry. A 100% land value tax corrects this injustice by returning to society what society itself created.

It is the fairest possible tax

Taxation should fall on things we have a legitimate moral claim to tax. Labor income is earned. Capital is produced by effort and saving. Consumption taxes burden everyday necessities. Sales taxes, payroll taxes, and income taxes all penalize productive activity in one way or another. A land value tax, by contrast, does not tax production, work, or investment. It taxes only the exclusive control of a naturally given resource whose value is socially determined.

This makes it uniquely fair. It aligns with the principle that no person should profit simply by owning what they did not produce. If a community builds a rail line, expands public services, and attracts businesses to a neighborhood, the resulting increase in land value should accrue to the public that generated it, not be pocketed as windfall gain by landowners. In this sense, a land value tax is not an arbitrary burden; it is a reclaiming of what was always morally public.

Taxing the unimproved value only is also crucial because it ensures that owners are not penalized for building homes, factories, offices, or farms. A person who improves land adds to society’s wealth and should not be punished for doing so. The tax falls only on location value—the pure rent of land—and thus targets privilege rather than effort.

It is economically efficient

From an economic standpoint, a 100% tax on land rent is uniquely efficient because land is perfectly inelastic in supply. Land cannot be hidden offshore, reduced in quantity, or moved to another jurisdiction. Whether taxed heavily or lightly, the total amount of land remains the same. That means taxing land does not distort the supply decision in the way taxes on labor or capital do. You cannot produce less land in response to a tax on land. As a result, the tax does not reduce productive activity in the economy.

This is one of the most important distinctions in public finance. Taxes on wages discourage work. Taxes on profits discourage investment. Taxes on buildings discourage construction. But taxes on land value do not discourage the creation of land, because no one creates land. They do not discourage development, because improvements are excluded from the tax base. Instead, they encourage the most efficient use of scarce locations.

When land is taxed based on its unimproved value, owners are incentivized to either use it productively or transfer it to someone who will. Speculative withholding becomes costly. Vacant lots in dense areas, derelict properties held for appreciation, and underused urban parcels become less attractive as passive stores of wealth. This helps reduce sprawl, increases housing supply, and promotes compact, efficient development near existing infrastructure. In short, a land value tax makes markets work better by aligning private incentives with social needs.

It reduces speculation and monopoly rent

One of the great failures of the present system is that land ownership often functions as a monopoly over access. In cities especially, the main determinant of wealth is not entrepreneurship but control over scarce locations. Owners can wait for rising prices, restrict supply, and extract economic rent from others who must live and work somewhere. This encourages speculation rather than production.

A 100% land value tax destroys the incentive to hold land idle for capital gains. If the full rental value of land must be paid annually to the community, then the owner gains nothing by waiting. Land will either be put to its best use or sold to someone who will. The economy becomes less about gambling on location scarcity and more about creating real value through work, innovation, and enterprise.

This is a profound improvement over systems that tax labor and enterprise while leaving unearned land appreciation untaxed. Under current arrangements, a developer may be discouraged by taxes on construction, while a speculator may be rewarded for sitting on valuable land. Georgism reverses this perverse incentive structure.

The claim that a 100% land value tax should be the sole source of government revenue is bold, but it follows naturally from the nature of land rent. Land rent is a surplus: it is the value left after accounting for labor and capital. In prosperous societies, especially where public infrastructure and dense economic activity create high location values, land rent can be very large. Capturing it fully provides a broad, stable, and growing revenue base.

Unlike income taxes, which shrink when the economy slows, or consumption taxes, which burden transactions, land rent is tied to the underlying value of exclusive access to natural opportunities and socially generated sites. As society grows and develops, land values tend to rise. Public revenue would therefore increase alongside prosperity, allowing government to finance essential functions without penalizing production.

If land rent is truly the surplus created by the community, then using it to fund the community is not only sufficient in principle but ideal in practice. Why tax wages, sales, or capital when society already generates a common revenue stream through land values? The state should not need to intrude into productive life when it can instead collect the value of exclusive site privilege.

It promotes affordable housing and better urban form

Housing affordability is among the most pressing social and political challenges in modern economies. Much of the cost of housing is not the structure itself but the price of the land beneath it, especially in desirable urban areas. When land values are privately capitalized and untaxed, they inflate housing prices and encourage owners to treat land as an asset class rather than a place to live.

One of the weaknesses of many existing taxes is that they invite avoidance, loopholes, and complex enforcement. Income can be hidden, profits shifted, consumption underreported, and capital moved. Land, however, is immovable and visible. Its location can be assessed. Its rental value can be estimated. This makes the land value tax unusually administrable.

Because the tax base is clear and tied to physical reality, it is difficult to evade. There is no incentive for elaborate accounting games over depreciation, offshore shelters, or fictitious losses. Governments could collect revenue with lower administrative overhead and greater public trust than under systems riddled with exceptions and manipulations.

Transparency also strengthens democratic legitimacy. Citizens can see what is being taxed and why. A tax on land rent is easy to explain: if you monopolize a valuable location, you pay society for the privilege. It does not seize earned income or personal property. It charges for a special privilege: exclusive access to a piece of the earth whose value arises from the community. Far from undermining freedom, it restores it by ensuring that no one can claim ownership over what nature and society jointly provide without compensating the community.

The moral logic is simple

At bottom, the case for a 100% land value tax is the case for justice over privilege. If one person earns a wage, it is theirs. If one person builds a house, the house is theirs. But if one person merely controls access to a location made valuable by everyone else’s presence and public investment, then the resulting rent belongs to the community.

George’s great insight was that poverty and inequality persist not because production is insufficient, but because the gains of progress are diverted into land rent. As society becomes richer, landowners often capture a disproportionate share of the increased wealth simply because they hold title to strategic sites. The remedy is not to punish success or accumulation, but to reclaim the socially created value of land.

A 100% land value tax accomplishes this elegantly. It eliminates unearned windfalls, discourages speculation, rewards productive use, and gives government a revenue source that does not damage the engine of wealth creation. It is simultaneously a tax, a reform of property rights, and a moral correction.

Conclusion

If government must exist, it should be funded in the least harmful way possible. A 100% tax on unimproved land value is that way. It is fair because it captures social value for social use. It is efficient because it does not distort productive decisions. It is practical because land cannot be hidden or moved. It is beneficial because it promotes development, affordability, and economic dynamism. And it is principled because it recognizes that the earth belongs, in common, to all people.

For these reasons, fully capturing land rent for public benefit is not merely defensible—it is the only tax policy that fully harmonizes justice and efficiency. If society is to fund its common needs, it should do so from the value that society itself creates. A 100% land value tax on the unimproved value of land, and the use of that revenue as the sole source of government finance, is the clearest expression of that truth.

The land is not a product of human labor. It is the common inheritance of all. No person made it. No person has a moral claim to extract income from simply owning a piece of the planet while others must pay to live and work upon it.

This is the central truth of Georgism: the Earth belongs equally to all people, and the economic rent of land should belong to all people.

A 100% tax on the unimproved value of land is not punishment. It is justice.

It does not seize the fruits of labor. It does not tax the sweat of the worker, the profits of the entrepreneur, or the value added by building, repairing, inventing, and improving. It taxes only the privilege of exclusive access to a natural opportunity whose value is created by society as a whole.

Imagine what this means.

No more speculation that leaves homes empty while families are priced out.

No more windfall fortunes from simply sitting on land while cities are forced to grow around idle holdings.

No more punishing productive work with taxes that discourage hiring, investment, and development.

No more rewarding the passive ownership of location over the active creation of wealth.

Instead, we would build a system where land is used efficiently, where prosperity is shared, where the community receives back what the community creates, and where government is funded by the one tax that cannot be escaped, hidden, or shifted onto labor.

And let us be clear: this is not merely a clever fiscal reform. It is a moral revolution.

It says that opportunity should not be hoarded.

It says that no child should be denied a future because someone else claims ownership over the ground beneath their feet.

It says that if society creates value, society should receive value.

It says that public services should be paid for not by penalizing work, but by collecting the community-created rent of land.

This would simplify our tax code, reduce corruption, encourage development, lower barriers to housing, and restore fairness to the economic order.

And perhaps most importantly, it would strike at the root of one of the oldest injustices in human history: the privatization of the common earth.

So let us be bold enough to say what others whisper and what powerful interests fear:

Fund government entirely from a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land.

Abolish private land rent.

Return to the people what the people create.

Let the gains of civilization flow to all, not merely to those who hold the deeds.

Let labor keep its full reward.

Let enterprise flourish without penalty.

Let land, the common gift of nature, serve the common good.

This is not radical in the sense of reckless. It is radical in the truest sense: it goes to the root.

And at the root of justice is this simple principle—

What no one made should belong, in economic value, to everyone.

Thank you.

Model Response:

The Earth Belongs to No One: The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax

How Capturing Land Rent Can Liberate Humanity from Poverty, Privilege, and Economic Stagnation

Introduction: A Question of Origins

Imagine inheriting a machine that prints money. You did not build it. You did not design it. You did not purchase the materials from which it was constructed. A great many people before you, and around you, contributed their labor, their ingenuity, and their social cooperation to create the conditions under which that machine operates. Yet by some combination of historical circumstance, legal convention, and inherited privilege, the machine sits in your basement, and every dollar it produces flows exclusively into your pocket. You need do nothing—not a single hour of productive work—to receive its output. You need only hold title.

This is not a thought experiment. This is the ownership of land.

Every day, the land beneath our cities, our farms, our coasts, and our forests generates enormous value—value created not by landowners, but by the communities that surround that land, by the public infrastructure that serves it, by the civilization that has collectively shaped it over centuries. In most nations, that value is captured almost entirely by private titleholders who did nothing to produce it. It is taxed modestly, if at all, and the rest flows into private hands as what economists call "economic rent." The result is a system of institutionalized extraction that impoverishes workers, distorts markets, fuels speculative bubbles, concentrates wealth, and forces governments to tax the very productive activities—labor and capital—that generate genuine prosperity.

There is a remedy. It was articulated most comprehensively by the nineteenth-century American political economist Henry George in his landmark 1879 work Progress and Poverty, and it has since attracted admirers ranging from Leo Tolstoy and Albert Einstein to Milton Friedman and Joseph Stiglitz. The remedy is the Land Value Tax—specifically, a tax of 100% on the annually assessed unimproved value of land, sufficient to serve as the sole or primary source of public revenue. Under this system, often called the Single Tax or Georgism, private individuals would retain title to the land they use, and would retain every dollar generated by their own improvements and labor upon it, but they would pay into the public treasury the full rental value of the land itself—the value created by nature and by society—returning it to the community that produced it.

This essay argues that a 100% Land Value Tax is not merely a viable policy reform but the most fair, most economically efficient, and most morally coherent approach to public finance ever devised. It is fair because land value is socially produced and cannot justifiably be appropriated by private parties. It is efficient because taxing the unimproved value of land does not distort productive behavior, discourages speculation, and encourages optimal land use. And it is sufficient because the aggregate annual rental value of land in developed economies is large enough to fund robust public expenditure without burdening the labor and capital that actually produce wealth. To allow private landowners to perpetually collect what belongs to all of us is an injustice—one that lies, as George argued, at the root of modern poverty itself.

Part One: Understanding the Nature of Land and Economic Rent

Before making the normative case for the Land Value Tax, it is necessary to establish clearly what land is, what land value is, and how it differs from other forms of wealth. Much of the hostility to Georgist ideas stems from a conflation of these categories—treating land as simply another form of capital, the ownership of which is as legitimate as owning a machine, a business, or a savings account. This conflation, as we shall see, is both economically confused and morally ruinous.

Land is Not Capital

In classical economics, the three factors of production were land, labor, and capital. Modern mainstream economics, with consequences that have proven disastrous for clear thinking about distribution and justice, collapsed land into capital, treating them as interchangeable inputs to production. They are not interchangeable, and the differences between them are decisive.

Capital is the product of past labor. A factory, a tool, a computer, a road—each represents stored human effort, directed toward productive purposes. Capital is created, and its quantity is not fixed. When entrepreneurs see profitable opportunities, they invest, and the stock of capital grows. When capital earns a return, that return compensates the effort and abstention involved in its creation—the labor of the workers who built it and the patience of those who deferred consumption to save, invest, and wait for results. Taxing the return to capital reduces the incentive to create it, and so imposes a real economic cost.

Land, in the relevant sense, is none of these things. Land—meaning the surface of the earth, its subsoil resources, the electromagnetic spectrum, the value of urban locations, and all other natural opportunities—is not the product of human labor. It was not created by anyone now living. Its total quantity is fixed. When a landowner earns rental income from land, that income compensates no productive effort, no creative act, no exercise of patience or forbearance. It compensates nothing except the historical fact of ownership. It is, in economic terminology, a pure rent—a return unattached to any productive contribution.

This distinction is not a semantic quibble. It has profound implications for both justice and efficiency, as we shall explore.

The Social Production of Land Value

Land value is not inherent in the soil. A plot of ground in the Mojave Desert has negligible value. The same square footage in downtown Manhattan commands millions of dollars per year in rental income. What accounts for the difference? Not anything the owner did. Not the quality of the soil or the subsoil minerals. The difference is produced entirely by society: by the density of economic activity in Manhattan, by the subway lines and roads and utilities that make the location accessible, by the courts and police departments that protect commerce there, by the culture and history that make it a desirable address, by the millions of workers and consumers and businesses whose collective presence generates enormous agglomeration economies. The Manhattan landowner collects rent because other people have created a city around the land. The desert landowner collects nothing because no such community exists.

Henry George's central insight was that land value is, at its core, a measure of the benefit that a location derives from the surrounding community. Land rent, in his formulation, rises as civilization advances—as populations grow, as infrastructure is built, as trade expands, as human knowledge accumulates—and this rising rent flows not to those who produced the advancement, but to those who hold title to the land. Every public investment, every population increase, every improvement in technology that raises the productivity and desirability of locations immediately capitalizes into higher land values—and those higher values flow to landowners who contributed nothing to produce them.

This is the mechanism George identified at the heart of what he called "the paradox of progress": the fact that widespread poverty and insecurity persist and often intensify even as material civilization advances. Workers and entrepreneurs produce wealth; landlords collect a growing share of it by virtue of their control over the natural opportunities without which production cannot occur. The laborer must pay rent to gain access to the earth. The entrepreneur must pay rent to gain access to a productive location. As the community grows and prospers, the rent that must be paid rises, and the share of output available to those who actually produce it diminishes.

Economic Rent as Deadweight for Society

To understand why the current arrangement is not merely unjust but economically destructive, consider the nature of an unearned increment in wealth. When a landowner in a gentrifying neighborhood watches property values double over a decade without lifting a finger or making any improvement, no new wealth has been created from that appreciation. The landowner has simply been awarded a larger claim on the wealth that others will produce in the future. This is a zero-sum redistribution from productive workers, entrepreneurs, and future landholders to current landholders. It enriches the few at the expense of the many, not through any productive mechanism, but through the bare fact of prior ownership.

Worse, the expectation of such windfalls actively corrupts the allocation of resources in a market economy. Rational actors respond to incentives, and when landholding offers handsome unearned returns, rational investors devote enormous resources to land speculation rather than productive enterprise. Capital that might have funded new businesses, new technologies, or new infrastructure is instead deployed in the purchase of land whose value rises partly because everyone else is doing the same thing. Speculative bubbles form, prices disconnect from productive value, and eventually—inevitably—they collapse, taking the broader economy down with them. The financial crises of 1873, 1893, 1929, and 2008 all bear the distinctive fingerprints of land price speculation, as documented by economists from George himself to the contemporary analyst Fred Harrison.

A 100% Land Value Tax eliminates the speculative incentive entirely. If the full annual rental value of land is returned to the public treasury, there is no surplus rent left for the private owner to capture. Land speculation becomes pointless. Holding land idle or underutilized becomes prohibitively expensive, because the full rental value must be paid regardless of whether the land is productively employed. Capital flows back toward genuine enterprise. The misallocation of the speculative economy is corrected at its source.

Part Two: The Justice of the Land Value Tax

The Lockean Proviso and Its Contradiction

The standard philosophical defense of private property rests on the Lockean argument that individuals acquire legitimate title to objects by mixing their labor with them and thereby creating value. A person who cultivates a field, builds a house, or fashions a tool from raw materials has a just claim to the product of their labor. This principle is widely shared across the political spectrum and forms the bedrock of both liberal and libertarian theories of property rights.

But it is precisely this principle that condemns the private appropriation of land value—and a clear-eyed Lockean should be among the most fervent advocates of the Land Value Tax. John Locke himself acknowledged the famous proviso: that the appropriation of natural resources can only be just if "enough and as good" is left for others. As the frontier closes and all land is claimed, this condition is violated for everyone born thereafter. The landless person is effectively told: the earth, which no one made, was entirely claimed before your birth, and you must pay rent to titleholders simply to stand upon it, live upon it, or work upon it. You must pay for the privilege of existing on a planet you had no hand in creating.

This is not the fulfillment of Locke's theory of just acquisition. It is its negation. Legitimate property rights exist to protect the fruits of human labor. The unimproved value of land is not the fruit of anyone's labor. Taxing it 100% does not violate property rights in any coherent sense—it simply recognizes that the value in question never legitimately belonged to the private titleholder in the first place.

Henry George articulated this with characteristic moral force: he advocated not the nationalization of land, not the redistribution of parcels, not any interference with the right to use and improve land and reap the fruits of those improvements. He advocated only for the community's right to collect the value that the community itself created. The distinction is crucial. Under a full Land Value Tax regime, a person who builds a magnificent building on a city lot retains every penny of rental income attributable to the building itself. They pay only for the underlying location value—the value that exists not because of the building, but because of the city. What is socially produced belongs to society. What is individually produced belongs to the individual.

This framework is more scrupulously respectful of labor and of genuine productive effort than our current system, which taxes wages, profits, and sales—the products of actual human activity—while leaving largely untouched the unearned increment that flows to landowners for doing nothing.

Left and Right Should Agree

The Land Value Tax occupies a rare position in political philosophy: it can be defended with equal force from both progressive and libertarian premises. From the progressive standpoint, it is the most direct possible intervention against the entrenched privilege of unearned wealth. From the libertarian standpoint—if that philosophy is taken to its logical conclusions rather than deployed selectively—it recognizes that no one has a legitimate claim to the value they did not create.

Milton Friedman, the patron saint of free-market conservatism, called the Land Value Tax "the least bad tax." But this undersells the Georgist case. The Land Value Tax is not merely the least damaging of a range of necessary evils. It is the only tax that takes nothing from its payers that was ever rightfully theirs. It cannot discourage productivity because it does not tax productivity. It cannot reduce the supply of land because land, by definition, cannot be created or destroyed in response to changes in its price. It is, in the precise technical language of economics, perfectly inelastic in supply—and a tax on a perfectly inelastic supply generates no deadweight loss, no economic distortion, no reduction in the total wealth of society.

This is not an approximation or a theoretical ideal that breaks down in practice. It is a mathematical identity. You cannot produce less land in response to a tax on land. The supply is what it is. The only change a Land Value Tax induces in the behavior of landowners is the elimination of the incentive to hold land idle or underutilize it—which is unambiguously a benefit, not a cost.

Addressing Generational Injustice

Consider what the current system of land ownership means in practice for successive generations. A person born into a family that holds substantial urban landholdings enters life with passive income—guaranteed by nothing but the historical fact of inheritance—that no amount of effort by others can create for themselves. A person born into a landless family must pay rent to gain access to any productive location, forever subsidizing the accumulated privilege of prior generations.

This is not a marginal phenomenon. In major metropolitan areas around the world—London, San Francisco, Sydney, Toronto, Tokyo—the majority of working-age adults cannot afford to purchase the homes in which previous generations lived on ordinary middle-class incomes, because the land value component of urban real estate has grown to dwarf the construction cost of the buildings themselves. Workers spend an ever-increasing share of their income on rent, not because housing has become more expensive to build, but because land has been permitted to appreciate without limit in the hands of those who already hold it. The wage gains of productivity growth are absorbed by rising land costs before they reach the workers who produced them. This is precisely the mechanism George identified 150 years ago, and it continues to operate today with extraordinary precision.

A 100% Land Value Tax would immediately curtail this dynamic. If the full rental value of land is taxed, holding land as a passive investment becomes economically worthless—what you hold is an obligation to pay rent to the public, not a ticket to receive it. Land prices would fall dramatically toward zero for unimproved value, because no rational purchaser would pay a capital price for an income stream they will not be permitted to keep. The speculative premium would evaporate. Housing would become affordable—not because the physical cost of construction changed, but because the parasitic premium of location speculation would be eliminated. First-time homebuyers, young workers, and families of modest means would find themselves able to purchase properties whose prices reflected only the genuine cost of building—the cost of labor and capital—rather than the arbitrary fortune of their historical moment.

Part Three: The Sufficiency of Land Rent as Public Revenue

One of the most common objections to the Georgist Land Value Tax—especially to the proposal that it serve as the sole source of government revenue—is that the revenue from land alone could not possibly fund the full range of modern government expenditure. This objection seems intuitive, but the evidence challenges it strongly.

Land Rent is Larger Than Commonly Appreciated

Economists who have attempted to estimate the aggregate annual rental value of land in developed economies consistently find figures that are substantially larger than is generally assumed. In the United States, assessments by economists including Mason Gaffney, Fred Foldvary, and Karl Williams suggest that the annual rental value of land—including surface land, subsurface resources, and the electromagnetic spectrum—amounts to somewhere between one-fifth and one-third of gross domestic product. In 2023, with U.S. GDP approaching $27 trillion, this implies an annual land rent on the order of five to nine trillion dollars. Total federal, state, and local government expenditure in the United States is approximately seven to eight trillion dollars annually. The numbers are, to put it plainly, in the right ballpark.

Several important factors push the estimate higher still. First, current land values are partly suppressed by the expectation that some LVT may be imposed in the future, and by the deadweight costs that the current tax system imposes on the economy. When counterproductive taxes on labor and capital are removed, the economy grows, incomes rise, and the demand for well-located land increases—which boosts land values and thus the revenue base of a Land Value Tax, even as it makes living conditions better for working people. Second, a comprehensive LVT would include currently undertaxed natural resource rents—oil, gas, minerals, fisheries, water rights, the electromagnetic spectrum assigned to private broadcasters and telecommunications companies—whose combined value is substantial and whose private appropriation is even harder to justify on principles of desert than urban surface land.

Third, and perhaps most importantly, the elimination of existing taxes on labor, capital, and consumption would produce substantial economic gains that would be partially reflected in higher land values. If the deadweight losses associated with income, payroll, sales, and corporate taxes—estimated conservatively at six to ten cents per dollar of revenue—were eliminated, the resulting economic expansion would generate higher incomes, more investment, greater productivity, and denser and more valuable economic activity in locations well-served by public goods. This virtuous cycle would tend to increase land rents even as it removed the burdens that currently suppress productive activity.

Prominent economists including Nobelist William Vickrey, who served as chair of the Columbia University economics department, have argued that land rent is sufficient to fund government. Joseph Stiglitz, another Nobel laureate, formalized what is known as the "Henry George Theorem," demonstrating that in an optimally functioning community, the aggregate land rents generated by public goods will equal the cost of providing those public goods. This is a theoretical result with profound practical implications: the very public investments that government spending provides are reflected, nearly coin-for-coin, in increased land values, which a Land Value Tax then captures and recycles in a perfectly self-sustaining fiscal loop.

Better Revenue from Better Sources

Even apart from the question of sufficiency, consider what the current tax system costs society compared to what a Revenue from Land Value Tax would cost.

When governments tax wages, they reduce the take-home pay of workers relative to the cost of employing them, which reduces employment and the incentive to work and learn. When they tax corporate profits, they reduce the return to investment, which reduces investment and capital formation. When they tax sales, they drive a wedge between buyers and sellers that suppresses transactions that would otherwise be mutually beneficial. Each of these taxes imposes a deadweight loss—a reduction in total economic welfare that benefits no one, representing transactions that would have occurred in the absence of the tax and did not occur because of it.

The peer-reviewed economic literature on the magnitude of these deadweight losses is sobering. Estimates range from ten cents to over thirty cents of economic damage for every dollar raised through conventional taxes. This means that a government collecting seven trillion dollars through income, payroll, corporate, and sales taxes is potentially imposing two to three trillion dollars per year in purely wasteful economic destruction—wealth that disappears into the inefficiency of distorted incentives, not wealth that is transferred to public purposes.

Land Value Tax has zero deadweight loss. The land exists; its supply does not change in response to price; the tax does not make it disappear or become less available. The revenue raised through LVT represents a pure transfer from private to public accounts with no surrender of economic efficiency, no suppression of productive activity, no distortion of the price signals that guide market decisions. Replacing existing taxes with a 100% LVT would therefore not merely be revenue-neutral in accounting terms—it would produce a massive improvement in economic welfare simply by eliminating the waste embedded in the current tax system.

Part Four: Practical Implications and the Path Forward

Urban Policy and the Efficient Use of Space

City dwellers know the phenomenon of the surface parking lot. In the heart of valuable, productive, densely inhabited cities—blocks from offices, transit stations, shops, and residences—land sits as nothing but asphalt, generating nominal revenue for its owner while sitting largely idle. Why? Because under current tax systems, the owner pays little or nothing to hold the land, while any improvement—any building that would put the land to productive use—is subject to property taxes on the full improved value, and to income taxes on any profits earned. The incentive structure actively encourages landowners to underutilize valuable urban land, withholding it from its highest and best use rather than paying the transactional costs of developing and improving it.

Under a 100% Land Value Tax, this calculus reverses completely. The owner of a surface parking lot in downtown Boston must now pay the full annual rental value of that location, regardless of whether the lot earns enough to cover it. Suddenly, withholding the land from development is extremely costly. The rational response is to either develop the land or sell it to someone who will. The result—dense, productive use of well-located urban land—is precisely what housing-constrained cities desperately need and have consistently failed to achieve through top-down zoning mandates, affordable housing set-asides, or any other conventional policy instrument.

The same logic applies to derelict industrial sites, underutilized agricultural land near urban areas, and underdeveloped commercial properties. A 100% LVT is the most powerful densification, infill-development, and anti-sprawl policy ever devised, not because it mandates any particular land use, but because it makes it economically irrational for landowners to hold valuable locations less than productively. The market then solves the allocation problem that government planning has consistently failed to address.

The Dividend Dimension: Georgism as Universal Basic Income

Henry George himself did not specify how the revenues from the Land Value Tax should be distributed, though he implied they should fund public services. But a compelling variant of the Georgist program—advocated by contemporary proponents including Peter Barnes, whose concept of "Cap and Dividend" echoes these principles, and academic Georgists like Fred Foldvary and Alanna Hartzok—proposes a "Citizens' Dividend" or "Land Dividend" in which a portion of LVT revenues is distributed equally to all citizens as a universal basic income.

The philosophical logic is compelling. If land value is a common inheritance—the gift of nature and the product of social cooperation—then every member of the community has an equal claim on it. A billionaire's claim on land rent is no stronger than an infant's. A Citizens' Dividend would provide every person, from birth, with a share of the value that belongs to humanity as a whole. This would constitute the most elegant and philosophically coherent form of universal basic income ever proposed, because unlike handouts funded by taxes on labor, it would not be taken from anyone's productive earnings. It would simply be the community's fair share of what belongs to the community, distributed to those who belong to it.

Alaska's Permanent Fund, which distributes oil revenues to all Alaskan residents, is an imperfect but real-world proof of this principle. It enjoys broad bipartisan support, has reduced inequality in Alaska relative to other states, and has provided a meaningful economic floor for the state's residents for decades. A properly designed Land Value Tax at national scale would generate revenues dwarfing the Alaska Permanent Fund, able to sustain a meaningful income guarantee for every citizen without requiring a dollar of conventionally raised taxation.

International Competitiveness

Critics sometimes worry that heavy land taxation would harm a nation's international competitiveness—that investors might take their capital elsewhere. But this objection confuses land with capital. Capital is mobile; it can and does flow across borders in search of better returns. Land cannot move. Manhattan's land will not relocate to the Cayman Islands in response to an LVT. The Marcellus Shale's natural gas will remain in Pennsylvania whatever the tax rate on its extraction. Agricultural land in Iowa will not relocate to a lower-tax jurisdiction. A 100% LVT is, uniquely, a tax from which evasion through capital flight is physically impossible. Landowners must either pay or sell, and the purchaser who buys from them faces the same obligation.

Meanwhile, eliminating taxes on capital, labor, and corporate profits would dramatically improve actual international competitiveness. Businesses locate in countries with skilled workforces, good infrastructure, strong institutions, and low taxes on productive activity. A Georgist nation would offer all of these: the productive benefits of densely populated, well-serviced cities funded by captured land rents, combined with zero income tax, zero payroll tax, zero corporate tax, and zero transaction taxes. As an environment for productive enterprise, this combination would be extraordinarily attractive. The 100% LVT effectively replaces a system that harms productive activity while rewarding passivity with one that supports productive activity while eliminating passive extraction.

Part Five: Responding to Objections

The Cash-Poor Landowner Problem

Perhaps the most sympathetic objection to a 100% LVT concerns the elderly widow or the modest farmer who holds land that has appreciated dramatically in value—not because of anything they did, but because of surrounding development—and who may lack the cash income to pay a tax on that appreciated value without being forced to sell. This is a genuine concern and should be taken seriously rather than dismissed.

But it does not undermine the case for the LVT; it simply requires thoughtful implementation. Several mechanisms address it. First, LVT obligations could accrue as a lien against the property, payable upon sale or bequest, rather than being demanded annually in cash. The farmer or retiree continues to use their land throughout their lifetime; at death or upon voluntary sale, the accumulated LVT is paid from proceeds. This is not substantially different from a reverse mortgage arrangement that many retirees already use. Second, rates could be phased in gradually over a period of years, allowing landholders to adjust their plans and for property markets to reach new equilibria without shock. Third, primary residences below a certain value threshold could receive partial exemptions during a transition period, preventing genuine hardship while still directing the full force of the tax against speculative and commercial landholdings.

These are technical accommodations, not concessions to the fundamental argument. The principle that socially produced value belongs to the community does not become less true because its implementation requires care. We should design policy to avoid unnecessary hardship, while insisting on the underlying justice of the reform.

Won't Landowners Simply Pass the Tax to Tenants?

Standard economic theory predicts that taxes are partly shifted from their nominal payer to other parties depending on the relative elasticities of supply and demand. For taxes on goods that are elastic in supply—goods that can be produced more or less in response to price—a significant portion of tax burden is shifted forward to consumers. But land, as we have established, is perfectly inelastic in supply. You cannot produce more land in response to demand. You cannot produce less in response to taxation. The full burden of a Land Value Tax therefore falls on the current owner and cannot be shifted to tenants.

The intuition behind this conclusion: if a landlord attempts to raise rents to cover an LVT obligation, tenants will seek alternative accommodation, the landlord will face increased vacancies, and rents in the market will not rise, because there is no reduction in the supply of rental accommodation—just a transfer of revenue from the landlord's income to the public treasury. The total amount of land available for rental remains exactly the same. Competition among landowners to find tenants keeps rents at the market-clearing level, which a LVT cannot move.

This is, in fact, one of the most socially valuable features of the LVT: it cannot be shifted to tenants or workers. Unlike property taxes on improvements, income taxes embedded in business costs, or sales taxes added at the register, the Land Value Tax has nowhere to go except to reduce the net income of landowners.

The Assessment Difficulty

How do we assess the unimproved value of land when improvements are inseparably present? Critics argue that because all land we observe is in some improved state—cleared, graded, accessed, served by utilities—it is impossible to determine what the bare land is worth without its improvements. This challenge is real but not insuperable.

Land assessors have been separating land from improvement values for over a century. Standard assessment methodology involves analyzing comparable sales of adjacent lots with varying levels of improvement, modeling the value gradient from highly-demanded central locations outward, and using hedonic price analysis to isolate location-specific factors from construction costs. Countries including Estonia, Denmark, Taiwan, and Australia, as well as many American municipalities including Pittsburgh and Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, have successfully implemented split-rate or pure LVT systems using exactly these techniques. Pennsylvania's experience is particularly instructive: cities that shifted their property tax base toward land and away from improvements consistently saw more construction, more rehabilitation of existing structures, and greater economic activity than comparable cities that did not.

Modern geospatial data, satellite imagery, machine learning, and real-time transaction databases have made land value assessment more accurate and more efficient than ever before. The technical difficulties that once seemed formidable are substantially resolved by contemporary computational and data resources. The assessment challenge is, in any case, a reason for care in implementation, not a reason to abandon the underlying reform.

Conclusion: The Moral Imperative of a Full Land Value Tax

Henry George wrote in the closing pages of Progress and Poverty with a moral urgency that still compels, more than a century after his death:

> "The great cause of inequality in the distribution of wealth is inequality in the ownership of land. The ownership of land is the great fundamental fact which ultimately determines the social, the political, and consequently the intellectual and moral condition of a people."

He was right. The private appropriation of land value—of the social surplus created by community and civilization—is the mechanism through which wealth concentrates in the absence of any productive contribution. It is the reason skyscrapers rise within sight of unhoused populations sleeping on sidewalks that privately owners refuse to develop. It is the reason that wage growth disappears into rising housing costs rather than improving the material conditions of working families. It is the reason that speculative bubbles form, economies collapse, and financial crises devastate the livelihoods of people who had no part in the speculation that produced them.

The 100% Land Value Tax is not a modest reform or a subtle adjustment. It is a fundamental reorientation of the relationship between society and the natural opportunities that belong to all of us. It says: what nature provides and community creates belongs to everyone. What individuals build and labor and invent belongs to them. This is not confiscation. It is restitution—the return to the community of what the community produced, freeing individuals to keep what they themselves made.

Such a reform would not require the apparatus of surveillance that income taxation demands. It would not punish work or productive investment or innovation. It would not create deadweight losses, capital flight, or bureaucratic complexity. A small class of people collects the rent of the earth. And because they collect it, the rest of us must work harder, pay more, and receive less than we have earned.

We do not need to smash the market. We do not need to nationalize industry. We do not need a bureaucracy to plan production or a government to tell you how to run your business.

We need to collect what was always ours.

The proposal is precise: tax the unimproved value of land at one hundred percent of its annual rental value — and use that revenue to fund every legitimate function of government, eliminating taxes on labor, production, sales, and buildings.

We tax only the underlying location value — the value that exists because of nature and community, not because of anything you did. The earth was not made for any one of us. It was not made by any one of us. Every acre of this planet that carries value carries it because human beings lived near it, worked near it, built roads to it, policed it, taught the children who grew up beside it. Georgism Revisited: The Case for a 100% Land-Value Tax
All land derives its value not from the labor or capital invested by any private owner but from nature, community infrastructure, location, and the collective progress of society. A 100% land-value tax (LVT) levied solely on that unimproved value would capture this community-created surplus—economic rent—and return it to the public that created it. In a Georgist framework, this single tax could replace all other levies, eliminating distortionary taxes on labor, production, and investment while ending the private appropriation of rent. The result would be a fiscal system that is simultaneously more just, dramatically more efficient, and fundamentally stabilizing.

Georgist analysis begins with a simple but powerful distinction: land is fixed in supply and passive; improvements and labor are elastic and active. David Ricardo observed that rent arises because different parcels differ in fertility or location; Henry George went further, showing that rent is a social product. The value of a corner lot in a thriving city is not created by the landowner’s shoveling and fencing; it is created by population density, schools, transit, police, courts, and the accumulated knowledge and expectations of millions of people. When that value accrues to a private title-holder, the rest of society pays twice: once in the purchase price or rent they must now afford, and again when the government raises taxes on their wages or sales to fund the infrastructure that generated the extra value in the first place. A 100% LVT dissolves this double charge. The tax collects the full annual rental value of the site and spends it on precisely the services that create the value. Ownership of land then becomes stewardship rather than a license to exact tribute.

Efficiency follows directly from the economics of incidence. Taxes on labor or capital reduce the net return to work and saving, shrinking the quantities supplied. A tax on land cannot shrink the quantity of land; its supply curve is vertical. The entire burden therefore remains on the landowner, who cannot pass it forward to tenants or workers. Occupiers still pay the same total outlay—part as explicit tax, part as reduced purchase price—but the economy loses none of the productive surplus that would have been destroyed by income, payroll, or sales taxes. Because the tax is levied on the highest and best use value, it exerts continuous pressure to develop sites at their optimal intensity. Speculative holding of vacant or underused urban land becomes expensive; owners must either improve it productively or sell to someone who will. The result is denser, more compact cities, reduced sprawl, lower infrastructure costs per capita, and fewer distortions in housing and agricultural markets.

Fairness is equally direct. No individual created the site rent of Manhattan or the wheat lands of the Great Plains. The first occupant merely happened to stake a claim at the frontier of settlement; later owners purchased an already-enhanced asset whose price incorporated capitalized community rent. Charging owners the full annual value they receive from the community is therefore restitution, not confiscation. Improvements remain untaxed. A family that builds a modest home or a factory that installs new machinery keeps every dollar of return above the rental value of the bare site. The progressive element is automatic: valuable central sites pay more, not because government imposes an arbitrary bracket, but because those sites command higher rents precisely because they benefit most from public services. Poor families on low-value land pay correspondingly little; many would pay nothing at all once their modest improvements are no longer encumbered by taxes.

The claim that LVT cannot raise enough revenue is refuted by empirical observation. In most developed economies the total economic rent of land—urban, suburban, rural, and resource-related—exceeds current government expenditure at every level. Studies of U.S. metropolitan areas have consistently found that unimproved land values alone, if taxed at full annual rates, would fund all local public services several times over; adding resource rents from oil, minerals, spectrum, and electromagnetic pathways widens the margin. The historical episodes of partial LVT—Pittsburgh’s graded tax, Australia’s state land taxes, and Taiwan’s system—demonstrate that even high rates do not collapse construction or ownership; they merely redirect capital from land speculation into buildings and equipment.

Because the tax base is visible, stable, and impossible to hide or move offshore, administration is simple and corruption-resistant. Assessors already estimate market values; separating land from improvement components is routine in every jurisdiction that uses modern computer-assisted mass appraisal. Owners cannot shift operations to low-tax countries because the tax follows the parcel, not the person or the corporation. Revenue predictability rises as land values track long-run population and productivity trends rather than volatile income or consumption.

Critics often object that an owner who paid a high price yesterday would be ruined by an overnight 100% tax. Georgist transition rules answer this concern. The tax can be phased in while simultaneously lowering or abolishing taxes on buildings and income; new purchasers would pay a price already net of the tax; existing owners receive an offsetting reduction in capital-gains exposure or a temporary credit. More importantly, the capitalized value of the land falls immediately upon credible announcement, transferring the present value of future rents from current speculative holders to the public fisc without any physical seizure. The burden is borne by those who bought an asset whose price already incorporated untaxed future rent. Subsequent buyers acquire land at a lower price and pay the ongoing tax; they are not disadvantaged.

A final, decisive advantage is macroeconomic stability. Land-value bubbles are the classic driver of financial crises. When land prices rise faster than productivity, households and banks load up on debt secured by appreciating collateral. A 100% LVT removes the incentive for such leveraged speculation. Land prices stabilize around the capitalized value of productive use rather than around expectations of further price increases. Credit cycles shorten, and resources that once flowed into land gambling are redirected into genuine capital formation.

Implementing a 100% LVT therefore aligns three objectives that most tax systems treat as trade-offs: equity, efficiency, and adequacy. It removes the penalty on human effort, captures the unearned surplus created by society, and funds public goods without shrinking the private sector. No other single reform promises so large an increase in both justice and prosperity. The moral claim is simple: what the community creates, the community should keep. The practical claim is equally clear: taxing land values at 100% of their annual rental worth is the only fiscal instrument that can do so without punishing work or stifling enterprise.

The inventor whose workshop sits on prime ground keeps every cent he earns from his invention, because the state no longer taxes his tools, his labor, or his creativity—only the privilege of occupying a finite slice of the planet. The farmer who clears new fields and enriches the soil pays nothing extra for his sweat; he pays for the land’s original fertility only, and keeps every harvest beyond that. Speculators vanish, because land ceases to be a vehicle for unearned gain. Cities grow outward in orderly beauty instead of sprawling into costly suburbs; poverty retreats because wages rise with the new demand for labor on every usable acre.

Some will object that this is confiscation. It is not. No one is stripped of what they made. Buildings remain private property; factories, homes, orchards retain their full market value and can be bought and sold without penalty. Only the publicly created value—the rise in price that results from population growth, public investment, and community activity—is reclaimed for the community that produced it. This is restitution, not robbery. This is justice.

History confirms it. Wherever even a fraction of land rent has been captured—whether Sydney, Brisbane, or the boroughs of Pennsylvania that tax land more heavily than buildings—housing becomes more abundant, investment in real improvements surges, and the gap between rich and poor narrows. Scale that principle to its logical conclusion, and the possibilities expand beyond measure.

Fellow citizens, we do not ask for charity. We ask for the restoration of our common inheritance. Let the full rental value of every acre, every city block, every waterfront—untouched by human labor—flow back into the public purse. With that single act we abolish involuntary poverty, unleash productive energy, and prove that democratic government can be funded without ever laying a hand on the fruits of honest toil.

Let the earth belong to those who use it, and let its rent belong to all.
