Model Response:

The Case for the Single Tax: Why Land Value Taxation Deserves a Place at the Center of Public Finance

A Persuasive Essay on Georgist Economic Reform

Introduction: The Tax That Asks the Right Question

Every civilization must answer a deceptively simple question: How should the wealth we create together be shared?

Most modern governments answer this question by taxing labor (income taxes), taxing trade (sales taxes and tariffs), taxing the products of human ingenuity (capital gains and corporate taxes), and taxing the very act of building and improving property. These taxes burden production, discourage effort, and distort markets. They punish people for working, saving, investing, and creating.

But there is one source of revenue that is fundamentally different — one that Henry George identified in his 1879 masterwork Progress and Poverty and that has since been endorsed by economists ranging from the libertarian Milton Friedman to the progressive Joseph Stiglitz. That source is land rent — the value that accrues to a location not because of anything the landowner did, but because of everything everyone else did.

A 100% land value tax (LVT) — a levy on the unimproved value of land exclusive of any buildings or improvements upon it, capturing the full rental value of land for public use — is not merely one good policy among many. It is, I will argue, the most economically efficient, morally defensible, and practically transformative reform available to any society. And it deserves to be the primary or sole source of government revenue.

I. Land Rent Is Unearned — and Therefore Unowned

The foundational Georgist insight is a moral one: no individual created the land.

Land — the physical surface of the earth and its natural endowments, including location, mineral deposits, access to water, and sunlight — was not produced by any human being. It is the common inheritance of all people, present and future. Every child born into this world has an equal moral claim to the gifts of nature. No one, by virtue of title or deed, has earned the right to monopolize those gifts and charge others for their use.

When a landlord in Manhattan collects $5,000 per month for a one-bedroom apartment, the vast majority of that rent does not compensate them for maintaining the building. It compensates them for where the building sits — for access to the subway system, the proximity to jobs, the cultural vibrancy, the safety provided by public services, the prestige of the address. All of those amenities were created by the labor, investment, and cooperation of millions of people. The landlord contributed nothing to their creation, yet captures the lion's share of their value.

This is what economists call economic rent — a return to a factor of production that exceeds what is necessary to bring that factor into productive use. Land rent is pure surplus. It exists because land is fixed in supply — no one can produce more of it — and because demand for desirable locations increases as civilization advances.

To tax this rent is not to confiscate anyone's earned wealth. It is to reclaim what was always collectively owned and return it to the community that generated it. As George wrote: "We must make land common property."

II. The Economic Efficiency Argument: The One Tax with Zero Deadweight Loss

Every tax creates some degree of deadweight loss — the economic value destroyed because the tax discourages the activity being taxed.

  • Income taxes discourage work and labor supply.
  • Corporate taxes discourage business investment.
  • Sales taxes discourage consumption and trade.
  • Property taxes (as commonly structured) punish people for improving their land, discouraging construction, renovation, and development.

A land value tax is categorically different. Land is fixed in supply. No matter how heavily you tax it, you cannot cause less land to exist. The supply curve of land is perfectly inelastic — a vertical line in economic terms. Because of this, a tax on land value cannot reduce the quantity of land, cannot distort production decisions, and cannot create deadweight loss.

This is not a fringe opinion. It is one of the most thoroughly established conclusions in public economics:

  • Milton Friedman called the LVT "the least bad tax."
  • William Vickrey, Nobel laureate in economics, stated that land value taxation "comes closer to being a perfect source of revenue than any other tax."
  • The 1990 Mirrlees Review in the UK concluded that a well-designed land value tax would be the most efficient form of taxation.
  • Joseph Stiglitz has argued that, under certain conditions, public investment is entirely self-financing through the land value increases it generates — a proposition known as the Henry George Theorem.

To put it simply: taxing land does not reduce the quantity of land. The landowner cannot pick up Manhattan and move it to Delaware to escape the tax. The tax simply redirects the land's rental value from private hands into the public treasury, without discouraging any productive economic activity whatsoever.

No other tax can make this claim.

III. The Development Incentive: Why LVT Creates Better Cities

Consider two adjacent parcels in a growing city.

  • Parcel A is owned by a speculator who leaves it vacant, waiting for land values to rise so they can sell at a profit. The land is unproductive, fenced off, generating nothing for the community — yet the owner benefits from the economic growth all around them.
  • Parcel B is owned by a developer who builds a mixed-use building with shops below and apartments above. The building serves hundreds of people, creates jobs, generates economic activity, and contributes to the vitality of the neighborhood.

Under a conventional property tax, Parcel B pays significantly more tax than Parcel A, because the tax is assessed on the value of the improvements — the building. Parcel A, with its empty lot, is lightly taxed. The system punishes productive use and rewards speculation.

Under a 100% land value tax, both parcels pay based solely on the value of their land. If both parcels sit on equally valuable land, they pay the same tax — regardless of what sits on top. This means:

  1. Speculators are forced to develop or sell. Holding land idle becomes financially punishing. The land must generate enough income to cover the tax, which means putting it to productive use.
  2. Builders are rewarded. Since improvements are untaxed, there is no penalty for constructing housing, offices, or shops. The incentive structure flips from "hold and wait" to "build and create."
  3. Urban sprawl is reduced. Because land value is highest in city centers, the tax incentivizes dense, efficient development where land is most valuable — reducing sprawl, preserving farmland and wilderness, and lowering infrastructure costs.
  4. Housing supply increases. When the tax forces vacant and underutilized land onto the market and removes the penalty on building, supply responds. More housing means lower rents.

This is not hypothetical. Pennsylvania allowed cities to implement a "split-rate" tax (taxing land at a higher rate than buildings) throughout the 20th century. Studies by economists like Oates and Schwab found that cities adopting the split-rate tax experienced faster development, less vacancy, and increased construction compared to neighboring cities. Harrisburg, which shifted heavily toward land taxation, saw its number of vacant buildings drop from over 4,000 to fewer than 500 over two decades.

Imagine what a full 100% LVT — not merely a split-rate adjustment — would accomplish.

IV. The Justice Argument: Poverty Amid Plenty

Henry George began Progress and Poverty with a puzzle that remains devastatingly relevant: Why does poverty persist alongside unprecedented economic progress?

In every era of technological advancement, from the Industrial Revolution to the age of artificial intelligence, we observe the same pattern: wealth concentrates, land values rise, and those without land or capital see their wages eroded by rising rents. The gains of civilization are captured not by the workers who produce them, but by the landowners who control access to the locations where production occurs.

This is not an accident. It is the logical consequence of a system that treats land — a finite, necessary input to all production and all life — as a speculative commodity.

When land values rise due to public investment (a new transit line, a school, a park), the increase in value flows entirely to private landowners. The public pays for the improvement through taxes; the landowner captures the windfall. This is a systematic transfer of wealth from the many to the few, subsidized by the very government that is supposed to serve the public interest.

A 100% land value tax reverses this transfer. It ensures that the wealth generated by community effort returns to the community. If government builds a subway line and land values along the route increase by $10 billion, the LVT captures that increase and recycles it into public services — or, if desired, into a citizens' dividend distributed equally to all residents, as Alaska does with its oil revenue.

This is the Georgist vision of justice: abolish all taxes on labor and production; fund government entirely from the value of the commons; and distribute any surplus equally as a birthright.

V. The Simplicity Argument: Replacing the Tax Labyrinth

The modern tax system is an obscenity of complexity. The United States Internal Revenue Code runs to thousands of pages. Compliance costs are estimated at $400 billion per year or more — a staggering deadweight loss imposed not by the taxes themselves but by the administrative machinery required to assess, collect, and enforce them.

A single tax on land value would sweep away this labyrinth. Land cannot be hidden. It cannot be moved offshore. It cannot be laundered through shell companies or parked in tax havens. Every parcel of land is visible, mappable, and assessable.

Modern geographic information systems (GIS), satellite imagery, and machine learning make land valuation increasingly precise and inexpensive. The assessment process can be made transparent, publicly auditable, and resistant to corruption. No more armies of accountants, no more tax shelters, no more annual filings that consume billions of hours of human attention.

This is not merely an administrative convenience. The complexity of the current tax system is a regressive feature — wealthy individuals and corporations can afford sophisticated tax planning that ordinary citizens cannot. A single land value tax is radically simple and therefore radically fair.

VI. Answering the Objections

Any serious proposal must confront serious objections. Let me address the most common ones.

"Won't landowners just pass the tax on to tenants?"

No. This is perhaps the most important insight in all of Georgist economics. Landlords already charge the maximum rent the market will bear. A land value tax does not increase the supply of land — it merely redirects a portion of the existing rent from the landlord to the public. The landlord cannot "pass on" a tax on something whose supply is fixed. The incidence falls entirely on the landowner, not the tenant. If anything, the LVT — by forcing idle land into use and stimulating construction — will lower market rents over time by increasing supply.

"What about elderly homeowners on fixed incomes?"

This is a legitimate concern with practical solutions. Tax deferrals, exemptions for primary residences below a certain value, or phasing in the tax gradually are all viable approaches. Moreover, in a full Georgist system, the revenue from the LVT funds a citizens' dividend that would more than offset the tax for most ordinary homeowners. The median homeowner in most cities sits on land worth far less than the per-capita share of total land value in the economy.

"What about agricultural land?"

Agricultural land, outside of areas facing urban development pressure, generally has low market value. The tax on a typical farm would be modest relative to its productive output. More importantly, by reducing speculation and sprawl, the LVT helps preserve agricultural land by directing development toward already-urbanized areas.

"Would this raise enough revenue?"

The total rental value of land in developed economies is substantial. Estimates vary, but several studies have suggested that land rent in the United States alone represents trillions of dollars annually — sufficient to replace all current federal, state, and local taxes. Even conservative estimates suggest the LVT could replace the majority of existing revenue sources. As land values rise with economic growth (and they reliably do, over time), the revenue base expands naturally, without ever needing to raise rates.

"Isn't this just confiscation of property?"

The Georgist position is that it is the current system that involves confiscation — the confiscation of the community's common wealth by private landowners. The LVT merely ends this confiscation. Landowners retain full ownership of their buildings, their businesses, and all the products of their labor. They simply pay rent for the exclusive use of a portion of the commons, just as a renter pays for an apartment. The "property right" being taxed is not the right to own the fruits of one's labor, but the right to exclude others from natural opportunities — a right that should be compensated, and that compensation belongs to everyone.

VII. The Moral Architecture of the Single Tax

At its deepest level, the Georgist argument is not merely economic but moral. It rests on a principle of equal liberty: every person has an equal right to access the natural world, and any system that denies this right must compensate those who are excluded.

The current system does the opposite. It grants a small number of landowners the right to monopolize the earth's surface — the most fundamental of all productive resources — and extract tribute from everyone else for the privilege of existing somewhere. It then taxes labor and trade, punishing the very activities that create wealth, in order to fund a government that subsidizes this monopoly through public investment that flows directly into landowners' pockets.

The Georgist alternative is a system in which:

  • Labor is untaxed. Every dollar you earn is yours.
  • Capital is untaxed. Every product of human ingenuity — your business, your inventions, your savings — is yours.
  • Land rent is shared. The value created by nature and by community investment belongs to the community.
  • Government is funded cleanly and sustainably. Revenue grows with civilization, without burdening productive activity.
  • Poverty is structurally addressed. As the economy grows, the citizens' dividend grows, providing a universal floor of economic security that requires no bureaucracy, no eligibility tests, and no stigma.

This is not utopian dreaming. It is a coherent, rigorously defensible policy framework that addresses inequality, stimulates development, simplifies governance, and honors the most basic principle of justice: what you make is yours; what we make together is ours.

Conclusion: The Question We Have Avoided

We live in an era of mounting crises — housing unaffordability, wealth inequality, urban decay, environmental degradation, political dysfunction. These crises are not unrelated. They share a common root in our refusal to reckon honestly with the economics of land.

We cannot tax our way to prosperity by burdening work and enterprise. We cannot address inequality while allowing the commons to be monopolized. We cannot build just cities while punishing development and rewarding speculation.

Henry George saw the remedy over a century ago. The economists who have followed — Friedman, Stiglitz, Vickrey, and many others — have confirmed its logic with modern rigor. The experiments that have been tried, from Harrisburg to Estonia to Taiwan, have demonstrated its practical viability.

The question is not whether the land value tax works. The question is whether we have the courage to implement it — fully, honestly, and without compromise.

The earth is the common heritage of all. It is time we acted like it.

"As civilization advances, the pinching of poverty becomes tighter and tighter. The cause is in the laws governing the distribution of wealth. To find these laws and apply them is the great labor of political economy." — Henry George, Progress and Poverty (1879)

Model Response:

Georgist economic philosophy, based on Henry George's work Progress and Poverty (1879), proposes that a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land—excluding any value from buildings, labor, or capital improvements—should be the primary or sole source of public revenue. This is often referred to as a Land Value Tax (LVT). Below are the purported benefits and reasons for this proposal, presented factually as they are argued within Georgist theory.

Core Principles of Georgism

  1. Distinction Between Land and Capital

    • Land: Includes all natural resources and spatial opportunities (locations, minerals, airwaves, etc.). Its supply is fixed and not produced by human effort.
    • Capital: Includes buildings, machinery, and improvements created by labor and investment.
    • Georgists argue that because land is a common inheritance, its economic rent (the value derived from location and natural advantages, not from owner effort) should belong to society collectively.

  2. Economic Rent as Unearned Income

    • Land value often rises due to public investments (infrastructure, schools, safety), population growth, and community development—not from the landowner’s actions.
    • Taxing this “unearned increment” is seen as morally just and economically efficient.

Purported Benefits of a 100% LVT as Sole Revenue

1. Economic Efficiency

  • No Deadweight Loss: Unlike taxes on labor, sales, or capital, an LVT does not discourage productive activity. Since land supply is fixed, taxing its value does not reduce its availability. This avoids the economic inefficiencies associated with income or corporate taxes.
  • Encourages Optimal Land Use: Owners must pay tax based on land value regardless of use, pressuring them to develop vacant or underused land (e.g., empty lots in prime areas) to its highest and best use, reducing urban sprawl and speculation.
  • Reduces Speculative Bubbles: By taxing land rent, holding land idle for speculative gains becomes costly, potentially stabilizing property markets.

2. Equity and Social Justice

  • Progressive Taxation: Land ownership is highly concentrated. An LVT falls disproportionately on wealthy landowners, making it inherently progressive.
  • Returns Common Wealth to Society: Since land value is created collectively, taxing it redistributes community-generated wealth to fund public services without penalizing individual labor or innovation.
  • Reduces Land Monopolization: Discourages land hoarding and could make land more accessible for housing or enterprise.

3. Simplification and Transparency

  • Single Tax Simplicity: Eliminating other taxes (income, sales, capital gains) would reduce administrative complexity, compliance costs, and opportunities for evasion.
  • Harder to Evade: Land is visible and immobile, making valuation and collection more straightforward than taxing capital or income, which can be hidden or moved offshore.

4. Environmental and Urban Benefits

  • Promotes Dense, Efficient Cities: By taxing land value rather than improvements, cities encourage vertical development and reduce urban sprawl, preserving natural habitats.
  • Aligns with “Polluter Pays” Principle: If natural resource extraction (e.g., mining, forestry) is taxed at its site value, it captures resource rents while encouraging conservation.

5. Macroeconomic Stability

  • Reduces Land-Price Volatility: By curbing speculation, an LVT could lead to more stable property markets and reduce boom-bust cycles.
  • Productive Investment Channeling: Capital might flow more toward productive enterprise rather than real estate speculation.

Common Criticisms and Counterpoints (Noted for Balance)

  • Valuation Challenges: Accurately assessing “unimproved” land value separately from improvements can be complex, though Georgists argue modern techniques (mass appraisal, market data) make it feasible.
  • Transitional Issues: Shifting abruptly to a single LVT could disrupt homeowners and markets; many Georgists propose gradual implementation.
  • Revenue Sufficiency: Depending on location, LVT alone might not cover all public expenditures, though proponents argue it could be sufficient if land rents are fully captured.
  • Political Resistance: Powerful landowner interests often oppose LVT due to concentrated costs.

Historical and Modern Context

  • Henry George saw this as a remedy for poverty amid progress, arguing it would eliminate “the great enigma of our times.”
  • Some cities (e.g., parts of Pennsylvania, Estonia, Denmark) have applied partial LVTs with noted effects on development patterns.
  • Modern Georgists often argue for LVT as a major revenue source rather than the sole tax, especially in mixed economies.

In summary, the Georgist case for a 100% LVT rests on arguments of economic efficiency, ethical fairness, administrative simplicity, and sustainable urban development, positioning land rent as the most logical and least harmful base for public revenue.

GERALD, 62 — "I Worked Hard for This Land"

Gerald bought a vacant lot in 1994 for $40,000. It is now worth $1.2 million because a hospital, three schools, and a light rail station were built around it — all paid for by other people's taxes.

Worked hard doing what, Gerald?

Gerald's position, distilled to its essence: "Society created all this value around my land, and I deserve to keep every penny of it because I exist near it."

PENelope, 45 — "What About the Poor Widows?"

Ah, the Poor Widow. She is the patron saint of anti-LVT argumentation. She is invoked in every debate with the solemnity of a prayer. She lives in a house she can no longer afford because the neighborhood has become desirable. She is in danger.

But Penelope is not interested in solutions. Penelope is interested in the widow. The widow is Penelope's emotional trump card, played with the confidence of someone who has never once Googled "land value tax deferral provisions."

When you explain the deferral mechanism, Penelope blinks twice and says, "But what about the poor widows?"

She means a different widow. There are apparently infinite widows. A Schrödinger's Widow, both protected and imperiled depending on what argument Penelope needs at the moment.

Derek has read exactly one book about economics. It was Atlas Shrugged. He read it at seventeen and has been insufferable ever since.

Derek's position: "If you tax land at 100%, that's basically the government owning all land, and that's communism."

Allow me to gently observe that communism involves the government owning everything you produce with your labor and capital — which is precisely what Derek is defending under the current system, where income tax, sales tax, and property tax on improvements all penalize productive activity.

This is not a flaw in the Developer. This is a flaw in the system. The Developer is acting perfectly rationally. The system is insane.

Under a 100% land value tax, the Developer would face a simple choice: build something useful, or sell the land to someone who will. Either way, the community benefits. The Developer benefits too, because he's no longer paying to hold land hostage.

But the Developer prefers the current system, where he sits on land like a dragon on gold, contributing nothing, and society thanks him for it by taxing the carpenters, the electricians, and the teachers instead.

The Developer is not a villain. He's an accountant who found the cheat code.

Susan bought her home for $200,000. It's now worth $600,000. Susan considers this $400,000 to be "her investment."

Susan did not build the new elementary school. Susan did not fund the park renovation. Susan did not personally lower the crime rate. Under a land value tax, Susan would pay more for her land but nothing for her house. Her improvements — the new kitchen, the solar panels, the landscaping she sweated over — would all be tax-free. The only thing taxed would be the unimproved land value, which she did not create.

Susan finds this outrageous. Susan feels entitled to the full $400,000 in community-created appreciation because she was standing on it while it happened.

Susan also wonders why young people can't afford homes. Susan has not connected these two thoughts. Susan may never connect these two thoughts. They exist in separate rooms of Susan's mind, and the door between them is locked.

THE INTELLECTUAL WHO IS "JUST ASKING QUESTIONS"

He writes for a mid-tier magazine. He is "not opposed to the idea of land value taxation, per se..." but he has concerns.

  3. "Isn't this politically unrealistic?" (Ah, the self-fulfilling prophecy. "We shouldn't advocate for this good policy because people like me keep saying it's unrealistic, which makes it unrealistic, which is why I say it's unrealistic.")

  4. "Wouldn't this cause... [gestures vaguely]... economic disruption?" (What kind? "You know. Disruption." No, we don't know. That's why we're asking. "Well, I'm just asking questions." You're not asking questions. You're casting doubt with a question mark at the end.)

The Intellectual concludes his essay by saying LVT is "worth discussing" and then never discusses it again, which is the polite way of burying an idea alive.

IN CLOSING

The opposition to a 100% land value tax is a beautiful tapestry of self-interest masquerading as principle, inherited assumptions dressed up as analysis, and emotional appeals that evaporate the moment you apply a single follow-up question.

The beauty of LVT is that it makes the argument for itself: the people who oppose it most vocally are, without exception, people who are extracting unearned rents from their community and would prefer to continue doing so.

And honestly? Fair play to them. They found the bug in the system. The rest of us just need to patch it.

The Land Belongs to All of Us

A Call for Justice in Taxation

Everywhere we look, we see the same disease dressed in different symptoms.

We see workers laboring harder than ever, yet falling further behind. We see young people priced out of every city their parents could afford. We see productive businesses crushed by taxes on their payroll, their sales, their innovations — while the owner of a vacant lot in a booming downtown sits on a fortune, contributing nothing, building nothing, and paying less in property tax than the café next door that actually serves people.

We have built an economy that punishes work and rewards speculation. We tax income — the reward for human effort. We tax sales — the engine of commerce. We tax buildings — the very structures that house and employ us. And then we wonder why housing is scarce, wages are stagnant, and inequality is a chasm.

Meanwhile, the one thing we should be taxing — the rental value of land, which no individual created — we barely touch.

Who created the value of a downtown parcel? Did the owner? No. The value comes from the subway built by taxpayers. The police who keep it safe. The schools that educate the workforce. The roads, the sewers, the parks, the hospitals — the entire architecture of civilization that makes that location desirable.

Society creates that value. And then we let private individuals capture it as unearned windfall — and tax the productive worker to make up the difference.

This is not a market outcome. This is theft, legalized by custom.

The Henry George Insight

In 1879, an American economist named Henry George published a book called Progress and Poverty, and he asked a question that still haunts us: Why does material progress produce poverty?

Why, in a world of increasing abundance, do we see increasing destitution? Why do our most productive cities become our most unequal?

George's answer was devastating in its simplicity: as civilization advances, the value of land rises — but that rising value flows not to the workers or the builders, but to the landowners, who did nothing to earn it. Wages are pushed down. Rents are pushed up. The gap between rich and poor widens, not because of differences in effort or talent, but because of a difference in access to a resource that belongs, by natural right, to everyone.

George did not propose taking land from anyone. He did not propose nationalization or central planning. He proposed something far more radical and far more respectful of liberty: tax the land value, and abolish every other tax.

No income tax. No sales tax. No corporate tax. No tariffs. No payroll levies. Just a single, annual charge on the value that land would command if left in its natural state — a value determined by community, not by the owner's labor.

Let me tell you why this is not just just — it is efficient in a way that should make every economist weep with admiration.

It cannot be evaded. You cannot hide land in the Cayman Islands. You cannot disguise its location. Every parcel is known. Every value is assessable. The tax base is literally under our feet.

It cannot be passed on. A tax on land value falls on the landowner. It cannot be shifted to tenants, because it doesn't reduce the supply of land — land is fixed. You cannot produce less land in response to a tax the way you might produce fewer goods. The land is there. The tax simply recaptures for the community the value the community created.

It does not distort incentives. Tax income, and you discourage work. Tax sales, and you discourage commerce. Tax buildings, and you discourage construction. But a tax on land value? It encourages landowners to use their land productively or sell it to someone who will. A vacant lot becomes a liability instead of a speculative asset. A parking lot in the city center suddenly faces real pressure to become housing or a business. The tax doesn't punish productivity — it punishes the withholding of a common resource from productive use.

It captures what the community creates. Every new school, every transit line, every park, every public investment — these raise land values. Under the current system, that value boost is a private gift from the public to landowners. Under Georgism, it flows back to fund the very services that created it. It is a self-reinforcing cycle of investment and return.

The earth is the birthright of every human being. No one made it. No one's labor can claim it. The Lockean tradition — the very foundation of private property rights — holds that we may claim ownership over that which we mix our labor with. You may own the house you build. You may own the crop you grow. You may own the business you create.

But the land itself? That was here before us. It will be here after us. It is the common inheritance of all humanity.

Thomas Paine argued that the earth is a common treasury and that ground rent rightfully belongs to the public. Winston Churchill — yes, that Churchill — declared:

The Georgist vision is not anti-market. It is the most pro-market reform imaginable. It says: go forth, produce, innovate, build, trade — and keep every cent you earn through your own effort. But the value that belongs to all of us, the value that no individual created, must be shared.

Imagine a world where land speculation — that great vampire on the neck of every city — collapses overnight. Where hoarding land becomes unprofitable. Where housing is built not where landowners choose to wait, but where people choose to live.

Imagine a world where the landowner of a skyscraper and the owner of a vacant lot next door pay the same tax, because the value is in the location, not the structure. And suddenly the vacant lot owner must build, must lease, must contribute — or sell to someone who will.

Imagine the revenue. Economists have estimated that the rental value of land in the United States alone — the unimproved value, stripped of all structures — amounts to trillions of dollars annually. This is not utopia. This is not fantasy. This is the system that dozens of economists, from across the ideological spectrum, have endorsed. Milton Friedman called the land value tax "the least bad tax." Joseph Stiglitz demonstrated formally that public investment in infrastructure pays for itself through increased land values — if only we recaptured that value. The Chicago School and the progressive left, for once in history, agree on something.

The Call

So I ask you: why do we continue to tax work instead of rent? Why do we punish the baker, the carpenter, the teacher, the nurse — while rewarding the speculator who produces nothing but scarcity?

Why do we accept a system in which a child born today is born into debt to the landowners who came before — a debt that grows with every public dollar spent to make this civilization livable?

It is time to reclaim what is ours. Not through force. Not through confiscation. Through the simple, just, and supremely efficient mechanism of a tax on land value — a tax that honors labor, unleashes enterprise, and finally delivers on the promise that the earth belongs to all of us.

The land is here. The value is here. The justice is waiting.

Let us have the courage to claim it.

The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax: Reclaiming the Earth's Bounty for All

In 1879, Henry George posed a fundamental question in his masterwork Progress and Poverty: "Why, in spite of increase in productive power, do wages tend to a minimum which will give but a bare living?" His answer—that private monopoly over land allows a privileged few to capture the fruits of social progress—led to one of the most elegant and just solutions ever proposed in economic theory: the Single Tax on land values. Today, as inequality reaches historic proportions and economic inefficiency plagues modern economies, George's prescription of a 100% land value tax deserves serious reconsideration as both the most equitable and efficient foundation for public finance.

The Moral Foundation: Land as Common Heritage

The case for fully capturing land rent begins with a fundamental moral principle: land, in its unimproved state, is the common inheritance of humanity. No individual created the earth, its natural resources, or its strategic locations. The fact that Manhattan Island sits at the confluence of great rivers, that Silicon Valley enjoys a Mediterranean climate, or that the Permian Basin contains vast oil deposits—none of these advantages stem from human effort. They are gifts of nature that belong, by right, to all humanity.

When private individuals are permitted to capture the rental value of these natural advantages, they are essentially collecting tolls on the birthright of every human being. The businessman who owns a downtown corner lot extracts wealth not from his own productive efforts, but from the community that has built up around that location. The landowner who holds pristine wilderness restricts humanity's access to its natural heritage. This is not merely inefficient—it is profoundly unjust.

Consider the alternative: when government captures 100% of land rent through taxation, it reclaims this common heritage for its rightful owners—the entire community. Every dollar collected from land values represents wealth that properly belongs to society, making its public capture not confiscation, but restitution.

Economic Efficiency: The Perfect Tax

From an efficiency standpoint, the land value tax stands alone among all forms of taxation as perfectly non-distortive. This remarkable characteristic stems from the fundamental economic reality that land, in its natural state, exists in fixed supply. Unlike labor, capital, or produced goods, the total quantity of land cannot be increased or decreased in response to taxation.

Traditional taxes create what economists call "deadweight loss"—they discourage the very activities we want to encourage. Income taxes reduce incentives to work and save. Sales taxes discourage consumption and trade. Corporate taxes drive businesses to relocate or restructure inefficiently. But a tax on land values affects only the price paid for land, not the quantity available. Since landowners cannot move their property to tax havens or reduce its supply, they must either use it productively or sell to someone who will.

This unique characteristic transforms the land value tax from a burden on economic activity into a powerful engine for optimal resource allocation. Under a 100% land value tax, holding valuable land for speculation becomes impossible—the annual tax would equal the full rental value, eliminating any residual gain from mere ownership. Land would flow to its highest and best use, urban sprawl would diminish as central land prices fall, and productive investment would replace passive speculation.

The Revenue Potential: Sufficient for Government Needs

Critics often question whether land rents alone could fund modern government operations. This skepticism reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of how land values reflect societal wealth. Land rent, properly understood, represents the "unearned increment" that flows to land from population growth, technological progress, and public investments. In thriving economies, this unearned increment is enormous.

Consider that in major metropolitan areas, land often comprises 40-80% of real estate values, even with improvements included. Manhattan land alone is worth trillions of dollars. Silicon Valley's astronomical real estate prices reflect the tremendous productivity and public investment concentrated in that region. Oil and mineral rights generate hundreds of billions annually. Agricultural land in prime locations commands premium rents based on fertility, climate, and proximity to markets.

Moreover, under a true Georgist system, land values would actually increase as other taxes are eliminated. Remove income, sales, and corporate taxes, and economic productivity would surge, driving up the rental value of land. Eliminate tax advantages for speculation, and land would be used more intensively, supporting higher populations and more economic activity. The tax base would be self-reinforcing: better public services funded by land rent would increase land values, which would increase land rent, enabling even better public services.

Historical examples support this potential. Countries like Denmark and Estonia have successfully implemented modified land value taxes, while cities like Pittsburgh saw remarkable economic growth when they shifted toward land value taxation. Singapore captures substantial land rent through public ownership, funding excellent public services while maintaining economic dynamism.

Justice in Taxation: End the Punishment of Productivity

Our current tax system embodies a profound moral contradiction: we penalize people for working, saving, investing, and trading—the very activities that create prosperity—while rewarding speculation and passive ownership. We tax the farmer's crops but not the land speculation that drives up farmland prices. We tax the wages of teachers and nurses but not the unearned increment flowing to downtown landowners from subway construction. We tax small businesses' profits while oil companies pay minimal royalties for extracting public resources.

This backwards approach to taxation violates basic principles of justice. Why should society punish the entrepreneur who builds a factory while rewarding the speculator who simply holds empty lots? Why should we tax away the wages of workers while allowing monopolists to capture the value created by the entire community's presence and investment?

A 100% land value tax would reverse these perverse incentives. Workers would keep their full wages. Entrepreneurs would retain their full profits. Savers wouldn't pay tax on interest earned through deferred consumption. Only those who extract wealth from mere ownership of natural resources—without contributing any productive effort—would face taxation. This represents true justice: the community reclaiming the value it collectively creates.

Addressing Common Objections

"What about farmers and elderly landowners?" The transition to land value taxation should be gradual, and hardship cases merit consideration. However, most farmer concerns reflect misunderstanding—productive agricultural land in remote areas typically has relatively low land value (as opposed to improvement value from buildings, equipment, and cultivation). Elderly homeowners could defer payment until sale or death. The social benefits of efficient land use and abundant public revenues far outweigh these transitional challenges.

"Won't this reduce development incentives?" Quite the opposite. By removing taxes on buildings and improvements while maintaining taxes on land, the system maximizes development incentives. Building a house or factory would face no tax penalty, while holding valuable land vacant would become prohibitively expensive. Cities would see more intensive development and lower housing costs.

"How do we assess land values separately from improvements?" While challenging, this is eminently feasible. Assessors routinely make such distinctions, and computer modeling can improve accuracy. The task becomes easier as the tax creates stronger incentives for precise valuation. Moreover, any assessment imperfections in a land value tax system would be far less economically damaging than our current web of distortive taxes.

The Transformation Ahead

Implementing a 100% land value tax as the sole source of public revenue represents more than tax reform—it would catalyze a fundamental transformation toward a more just and prosperous society. Urban sprawl would give way to vibrant, compact communities. Housing would become more affordable as land speculation endings. Economic inequality would decrease as unearned wealth transfers ended. Innovation and hard work would receive their full reward, while passive rent-seeking would disappear.

Environmental benefits would be equally dramatic. Sprawl-reducing incentives would preserve wilderness and farmland. Resource extraction would face appropriate taxation, encouraging conservation and efficiency. Urban intensification would reduce transportation needs and energy consumption.

Perhaps most importantly, this transformation would restore the fundamental social compact: that those who benefit from common resources contribute proportionally to common needs, while those who create genuine value through their efforts are free to enjoy the full fruits of their labor.

Conclusion: Reclaiming Our Birthright

Henry George observed that "the equal right of all men to the use of land is as clear as their equal right to breathe the air—it is a right proclaimed by the fact of their existence." Today, as billions struggle in poverty while landowners grow rich through mere ownership, as productive workers face crushing tax burdens while speculators pay nothing on their unearned gains, George's vision remains both radical and essential.

The 100% land value tax offers a path toward an economy that rewards contribution rather than extraction, that provides abundance rather than artificial scarcity, that recognizes shared inheritance rather than privileged monopoly. It promises adequate public revenue without economic distortion, environmental protection without sacrificing prosperity, and social justice without compromising individual freedom.

The earth belongs to all humanity. The wealth that flows from this common heritage should support our common needs. The time has come to stop subsidizing speculation and start rewarding contribution, to stop punishing productivity and start capturing land rent, to stop accepting inequality as inevitable and start building the just society that remains within our grasp. The single tax on land values—implemented fully and completely—represents not merely sound policy, but a moral imperative whose time has come.

Model Response:

The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax

A just tax system should meet three basic tests. It should not punish productive work. It should not reward privilege or speculation. And it should finance public needs by collecting value that the public itself creates. A 100% tax on the unimproved rental value of land—paired with the abolition of taxes on labor, trade, buildings, and investment—meets all three tests better than any alternative.

This is the central insight of Georgist economics. Individuals should own what they create, but no individual created the earth. Buildings, crops, machines, and businesses are products of labor and capital. Land, natural opportunities, and location values are not. Although people may properly enjoy secure possession of particular sites, the economic rent of those sites arises largely from nature, population, public investment, and the activity of the surrounding community. Fully capturing that rent for public use is therefore not confiscation of private production. It is the recovery of a socially generated value for the society that generated it.

Land Rent Is the Proper Source of Public Revenue

The “land value” in a land value tax does not include houses, factories, shops, crops, drainage, or other improvements. It means the value of the site in its unimproved condition: what someone would pay for the exclusive use of that location, apart from structures and other privately created assets.

Consider two physically identical vacant lots. One stands in a remote area with few roads, jobs, or services. The other stands in the center of a prosperous city, near transit, schools, utilities, parks, customers, and millions of potential collaborators. The second lot may be worth a thousand times more, but its owner did not create that difference. The difference reflects access to the community.

Land prices rise when the population grows, when businesses cluster together, when government builds infrastructure, and when neighbors improve the surrounding area. A new railway station, for example, can add enormous value to nearby sites even if their owners do nothing. Under conventional finance, the public pays for the station through taxes on wages and commerce, while landowners receive much of the resulting increase in location value. Society effectively charges workers for creating an unearned windfall for titleholders.

A 100% land value tax reverses this injustice. The public investment still benefits the area, but the resulting increase in land rent returns to the public treasury. Those who improve their property retain the full value of their improvements. Those who merely control a scarce location cannot privately appropriate the value created around it.

Full Collection Is Fairer Than Partial Collection

A modest land value tax would be better than taxes on work and investment, but Georgist principles support collecting the full economic rent. The ethical claim is not that society deserves an arbitrary portion of land rent. It is that equal membership in society gives everyone an equal claim to the value of natural opportunities.

Private title can provide secure, transferable possession without granting the owner an unlimited right to absorb socially created rent. Under full land-rent collection, occupants would still choose how to use sites, sell buildings and improvements, and transfer possessory interests. What they could not sell for a windfall would be the capitalized privilege of withholding a location from everyone else while keeping its community-created value.

This system is especially fair because it separates earned from unearned income. A person who builds a home, opens a shop, invents a product, or improves a farm creates additional wealth and should retain the return. A person whose vacant lot appreciates because others build a thriving city around it has not created that increase. Taxing the former while exempting the latter is morally backward.

Full land-rent collection also gives practical substance to the idea that the earth belongs equally to all. Equal rights to land cannot mean that every person must receive an identical physical parcel; parcels differ radically in fertility, resources, and location. Equality can instead be achieved by allowing exclusive possession while requiring possessors to compensate the community for the value of the opportunities they exclude others from using. The land value tax is thus not a penalty on ownership. It is payment for exclusive access to a common inheritance.

Unlike Ordinary Taxes, It Does Not Shrink the Tax Base

Most taxes discourage whatever they fall upon. Taxes on wages make employment less rewarding and more expensive. Payroll taxes discourage hiring. Sales taxes reduce exchange. Taxes on buildings discourage construction and maintenance. Taxes on business profits penalize successful investment. Tariffs obstruct specialization and raise consumer prices.

A tax on the unimproved value of land is fundamentally different because the supply of land is fixed. Taxing land does not cause less land to exist. A valuable urban site cannot move abroad, disappear into an offshore account, or be produced in smaller quantities because it is taxed. The same site remains available for use.

This gives land value taxation an exceptionally low deadweight cost. The tax does not reduce the return to constructing a building because the building is excluded from assessment. It does not reduce the wage earned by working because labor is untaxed. It does not reduce the reward for producing machinery or starting a firm because capital and enterprise are untaxed. It falls instead on economic rent: income above what is necessary to bring land into existence, which is zero because nobody produces land.

Although owners would remit the charge, they generally could not pass a pure land value tax on to tenants in the way they might pass along a tax that constrains new construction. Rent is already set by what users are willing to pay and by competing locations. A landlord cannot sustainably raise the market rent merely because the tax bill rises; if the site could command more, the landlord could normally have charged more before the tax. The principal effect is to redirect land rent from private recipients to the public.

It Would End Land Speculation and Encourage Development

Present systems reward owners for withholding valuable land while waiting for the community to increase its price. Empty lots can sit beside crowded neighborhoods. Derelict buildings can remain in growing commercial districts. Urban expansion can leap over undeveloped parcels, forcing longer commutes and higher infrastructure costs. The owner profits not by producing something, but by delaying production.

A 100% land value tax would remove this speculative prize. Because the annual rental value of the site would be publicly collected whether or not the site were used, owners would have a strong incentive either to put land to its most appropriate permitted use or transfer it to someone who would. Keeping a prime urban parcel vacant would no longer be a cheap wager on future appreciation.

At the same time, removing taxes from buildings would eliminate a major penalty on development. Under ordinary property taxation, constructing apartments or renovating a shop raises the tax bill. A pure land value tax does the opposite: the site charge remains based on land value, while improvements remain untaxed. Owners are therefore encouraged to build, repair, expand, and maintain.

The combined result would be more compact development, less sprawl, more housing in high-demand areas, shorter travel distances, and more efficient use of existing infrastructure. Land would tend to flow toward those able to use it productively rather than those best positioned to hold it passively.

It Would Make Housing More Affordable

A land value tax is not a complete substitute for sensible planning and housing policy, but it addresses a central cause of high housing costs: the privatization and capitalization of scarce location value.

When future land rent can be privately retained, buyers bid that expected income into the purchase price of land. High land prices then increase the cost of acquiring sites for housing. Credit expansion can intensify the process, sending borrowed money into a fixed supply of locations and producing speculative booms.

If the full rental value of land is collected publicly, the speculative selling price of bare land tends toward zero, because purchasers no longer buy the right to keep future land rent. They would still pay for buildings and other improvements, and they would owe the recurring site charge, but they would not need to finance a large private purchase price for the land privilege itself.

This distinction matters. A recurring payment does not automatically make occupancy costless, but it changes who receives the payment and eliminates the capitalized speculative windfall. Revenue can replace taxes embedded in construction, wages, goods, and services—or be returned equally as a social dividend. Meanwhile, the incentive to develop underused sites expands housing supply where demand is strongest.

The result is a housing system less burdened by speculation, less punitive toward construction, and less likely to enrich owners merely because population and public investment raise the value of their locations.

Public Infrastructure Could Become Largely Self-Financing

Georgist finance creates a powerful alignment between public investment and public revenue. Infrastructure and public services often increase nearby land values. Transit improves accessibility. Parks add amenity value. Flood protection makes land safer. Schools, sanitation, and public order make locations more desirable. Under conventional taxation, governments frequently finance these benefits by taxing production, while the associated land-value gains accrue privately.

Under full land-rent collection, the community recovers the value its investments create. A useful infrastructure project can expand the land-rent base, allowing the public to finance improvements without imposing additional burdens on labor and enterprise. Governments would gain a clearer financial incentive to make places genuinely more useful rather than merely to distribute subsidies.

This does not mean every public project is justified whenever nearby land values rise. Public decisions must still account for equity, environmental effects, displacement, and long-term costs. But land-rent collection closes the fiscal loop: public value creation produces public revenue.

It Would Reduce Inequality Without Penalizing Success

Modern inequality is often attributed entirely to differences in talent, effort, education, or saving. Yet a substantial share arises from ownership of scarce assets whose value increases because society grows around them. Land ownership can generate gains unrelated to productive contribution, and those gains are often leveraged across generations.

This has a cumulative effect. Those who already own valuable land receive rising rents and collateral values. They can borrow against those gains to acquire more property. Those without land must pay rent from wages already reduced by income and payroll taxes. The tax system therefore burdens earned income while reinforcing ownership-based privilege.

A land value tax attacks this pattern at its root. It does not cap wages, confiscate factories, or penalize invention. It simply socializes the rent of a resource no individual made. Productive inequality—the difference between those who create more and those who create less—can remain. Privilege based on monopolizing natural opportunities cannot.

If land revenue exceeded the cost of essential government, the surplus could be distributed equally as a citizen’s dividend. Every person would then receive a tangible share of the value of the common inheritance. This would provide a universal floor without imposing marginal taxes on work.

It Could Stabilize the Economy

Land speculation plays a major role in financial instability. When credit expands, much of it flows not into creating new productive assets but into bidding up the price of existing land. Rising land prices increase collateral values, which support more lending and still higher prices. Eventually debt service outruns incomes, prices reverse, and the banking system contracts.

Full collection of land rent would sharply reduce the capitalized selling price of land and therefore its attractiveness as a speculative asset. Banks would have less reason to finance purchases based primarily on expectations of site appreciation. Credit would be more likely to support buildings, equipment, inventories, and enterprises—assets that can actually be produced.

Because land cannot vanish or flee, its rent also provides a relatively durable revenue base. Assessments would need to be updated regularly, and revenues would still vary with local conditions, but the base is inherently more observable and immovable than profits shifted among jurisdictions or income hidden through elaborate accounting.

Administrative Challenges Are Real but Solvable

The strongest practical objection is assessment: land and buildings are usually sold together, so how can officials determine the unimproved value of the site?

The task requires competent administration, but it is neither mysterious nor unprecedented. Assessors can use vacant-land sales, comparable sites, redevelopment transactions, ground leases, construction costs, capitalization methods, geographic information systems, and statistical models. Because neighboring land values generally vary in systematic spatial patterns, mass appraisal can estimate them with increasing precision. Owners should have transparent access to the data and a robust right of appeal.

No tax base is perfectly measured. Income taxes depend on contested definitions of income, depreciation, residence, deductions, transfer pricing, and realization. Sales taxes require classification and collection across millions of transactions. Corporate taxes invite complex avoidance. Compared with these systems, land is conspicuous, permanent, and impossible to conceal.

A transition would nevertheless require care. People who purchased land under the old system paid prices reflecting the expectation of future private rent. Immediate full collection would reduce those asset values and could create hardship for some heavily indebted or land-rich but cash-poor households. A credible phase-in, deferral arrangements for qualifying occupants, and banking reforms could address transition costs without surrendering the principle. Deferrals should be liens settled upon sale or transfer, not exemptions that recreate privilege.

Assessment must also distinguish genuine land value from improvements and avoid charging owners for value they themselves created. Clear standards, independent review, and periodic reassessment are essential. These are arguments for sound implementation, not for continuing to tax labor and investment.

Why It Should Be the Sole Tax

If land rent is sufficient to finance legitimate public functions, there is no principled reason to retain taxes that penalize production. Abolishing income, payroll, sales, corporate, and improvement taxes would remove enormous compliance costs and eliminate many opportunities for evasion, favoritism, and political manipulation.

The single-tax principle also disciplines government. Public revenue would be tied to the value of the common domain rather than to an open-ended claim on every private transaction. Government would prosper when communities became safer, more accessible, and more productive—not merely when tax rates rose or enforcement became more intrusive.

The case for land rent as the sole ordinary source of public revenue does not require pretending that implementation is mechanically simple or that revenue needs are identical everywhere. It asserts a hierarchy of claims. Before government taxes anyone’s work, purchases, savings, or buildings, it should collect the economic rent of land and other natural opportunities. Charges for specific scarce resources, pollution, and publicly created privileges fit the same Georgist logic: payment for exclusive use or imposed social cost, not taxation of productive effort.

If public land rent were fully collected, governments would gain a broad and economically efficient revenue base. Where collections exceeded expenditure, the remainder should be returned equally rather than used to justify waste. Where ordinary public needs exceeded land rent, the first response should be to examine spending, public asset management, and the capture of other monopoly rents—not reflexively to tax labor.

Common Objections Fail

One objection says that landowners “earned” their property by purchasing it. But a purchase transfers an existing legal claim; it does not establish that the underlying rent was rightfully privatized in the first place. Buying a privilege in good faith may justify transitional protection, but it cannot make the privilege permanently just.

Another says the tax would destroy property rights. In reality, it would clarify them. People would retain strong rights to possess land, transfer occupancy, and own every improvement they create. What would disappear is the right to appropriate the community-generated rental value of a natural opportunity. Property in products of labor would become more secure because government would no longer need to tax those products.

A third objection says the tax would be passed on to renters. But market rents are governed by demand, supply, and location. A tax on a fixed supply of land does not reduce that supply. Indeed, by discouraging vacancy and exempting construction, it can expand the supply of usable housing and commercial space. While leases and transitional market conditions can complicate short-run incidence, the long-run burden falls chiefly on landowners through reduced land prices and captured rent.

A final objection says a 100% rate leaves no margin for error. This is a legitimate administrative caution, not a refutation of the goal. In practice, “100%” should mean collection of the reliably assessed economic rent, not a demand that officials pretend to impossible precision. Conservative valuation, frequent reassessment, averaging provisions, and appeals can prevent accidental overassessment while moving toward full capture.

Conclusion

The central question of taxation is not merely how government can raise money. It is which values belong to individuals and which belong to the community.

Wages belong to workers. The returns to buildings, machines, and businesses belong to those who create and finance them. But the rental value of land arises from a common natural inheritance and from the presence, investment, and activity of society. Allowing individuals to keep that value while taxing labor and production is both unjust and economically destructive.

A 100% tax on unimproved land value would recover public value for public purposes, discourage speculation, stimulate construction, lower the speculative price of land, reduce inequality, support infrastructure, and replace taxes that suppress work and exchange. It would preserve secure private possession while denying private claims to socially created rent. Properly phased in and transparently administered, it would provide the fairest and most efficient foundation for public finance.

The Georgist principle can be stated simply: what people create should belong to them; what no person created, and what the whole community gives value to, should benefit everyone. A government financed by land rent would align taxation with that principle—and replace a system that penalizes contribution with one that charges for privilege.

Prompt:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of implementing a 100% land value tax on the unimproved value of land, based on Georgist economic principles, emphasizing why fully capturing land rent for public benefit is fair, efficient, and should be the sole source of government revenue.
Model Response:

Implementing a 100% land value tax (LVT) on the unimproved value of land—a tax on the economic rent of location rather than on labor or improvements—is one of the most compelling public finance reforms ever proposed. Rooted in Georgist economic principles, a fully implemented LVT is not merely a policy tweak; it is a coherent system that recognizes a basic moral and economic truth: the value of land is created by society, not by the landowner’s personal effort. Therefore, the public should capture that value for the public good. Doing so can be both fair (because it targets unearned privilege), and efficient (because it does not discourage production), and it can even serve as the sole source of government revenue (because land rent is the most stable and broadly shared base available).

1. The moral case: land value is unearned, and capturing it is fair

Georgism begins with a moral insight: most land value is not produced by the owner. The unimproved value of land reflects factors like:

  • proximity to jobs, schools, and transit,
  • the presence of markets and businesses,
  • neighborhood growth and civic investment,
  • population density and cultural development,
  • the continued existence and effectiveness of law and property institutions.

These are not acts of private creation by the landowner. A plot’s value rises largely because society grows around it and because public systems make economic life possible. In other words, land value is largely the result of collective development and public order, not individual effort.

A 100% LVT is therefore fair because it targets economic rent—the surplus people pay simply to access a scarce natural opportunity. This rent is “unearned” in the sense that it is not proportional to what the owner contributed. The landowner may have purchased rights, but the magnitude of the rent typically grows with society’s success. To tax that rent is to align private property with public justice: the benefit of social progress should return to society, not accrue automatically to owners without their participation in production.

Critically, this is a different moral logic from conventional property taxes. Taxes on houses and improvements resemble taxing the output of labor and investment. By contrast, a land value tax resembles a payment for using a common resource whose value is socially generated. It is less like penalizing success and more like collecting a social dividend.

2. The efficiency case: a LVT does not distort productive behavior

A common objection to taxation is that it punishes work and investment. Georgist economics answers that the choice of tax base matters.

A. Land supply is fixed, so taxing its value cannot shrink it

Land is immobile and limited. Even if taxes increase, owners cannot create more coastline, more urban adjacency, or more mineral deposits. Because the supply is fixed, the landlord cannot respond by producing less land. Instead, a land value tax largely affects ownership returns, not the availability of land.

This is the central Georgist efficiency claim: taxing land rent does not create a classic economic deadweight loss, because the taxed base cannot be meaningfully reduced.

B. Improvements are left untouched, so incentives remain strong

Under a tax system that includes buildings, roads, and other improvements, owners are pressured not to build or improve. A 100% LVT on unimproved value avoids that problem. If someone invests in a building, they increase the value of the property’s improvements—not the unimproved land base. As a result, the incentive is aligned:

  • Better buildings and productive use can increase the overall return to the owner.
  • There is no direct tax penalty for development and modernization.
  • The tax does not discourage productive activity because it does not tax the results of human effort.

In practical terms, a fully implemented LVT tends to reward improvements and productive use of sites, while discouraging land hoarding and speculative vacancies—situations where land is withheld from use because its market value rises without development.

C. Speculation and wasteful holding lose their advantage

Where land values rise rapidly, owners may hold land unused in anticipation of future appreciation. A 100% LVT would capture that appreciation as it occurs. That reduces the payoff to waiting without developing and encourages land to be used in ways that satisfy demand.

Importantly, this is not just a financial adjustment; it is a reallocation of resources toward socially valuable activity. When land is costly to hold idle, owners either develop it, lease it productively, or sell it to others who will. The community benefits from more usable space, better housing availability, and more vibrant local economies.

3. Why 100% of land rent: it’s the cleanest path to a single-source revenue system

Georgists often argue for the full taxation of land rent because partial capture leaves too much of the economic rent to private extraction and allows distortions and gaming to persist. Capturing 100% of unimproved value does several things at once:

  1. Neutralizes unearned advantage: If land rent is the unearned surplus created by society, taxing it fully prevents landlords from siphoning it off while making no additional contribution.
  2. Removes the need for other distortive taxes: Income taxes, payroll taxes, sales taxes, and corporate taxes can discourage work, hiring, consumption, or investment. If land rent can fund the state adequately, the government can eliminate those distortions.
  3. Stabilizes public finance: Land rent tends to persist even as productivity and consumption patterns change. As long as society remains prosperous and urbanized, location values generate a reliable tax base.

From a Georgist perspective, land rent is uniquely suited to fund government because it is the share of wealth linked to socially produced opportunity, not private production. Fully capturing it is not only efficient; it is constitutionally and economically consistent with the role of government: to protect freedom, enforce property and contract, and provide collective goods.

4. “Should be the sole source of government revenue”: the logic for replacing all other taxes

Replacing all government revenue with a 100% LVT is persuasive not because it is merely simpler, but because it rests on a principled economic separation:

  • Government revenue should come from unearned sources (like land rent),
  • while the market should be left largely to tax-and-subsidy-free incentives for production.

A wide variety of taxes—especially on labor and capital—create friction. They reduce the private gains from productive activity, and the result is an economy that grows more slowly than it otherwise could. By contrast, a land value tax targets a base that does not decrease when people work, invent, or build; if anything, it encourages those activities by leaving improvements untaxed.

Moreover, a sole-revenue LVT would be administratively coherent. Once land values are assessed, the government can operate with predictable funding. The tax is also relatively broad: practically every jurisdiction has land, and land values across neighborhoods reflect demand generated by collective life.

5. Addressing fairness and transition concerns

A serious argument for a full LVT should also address fairness in implementation. Critics sometimes worry that owners who purchased land under the old system will face sudden losses. Georgists typically respond with two points:

  1. The land value being taxed is not the value of the improvements and not the result of recent labor or investment by the owner. It is fundamentally the value of location and scarcity, largely created by society.
  2. Transition measures can be designed so that the policy is phased in or paired with mechanisms that prevent hardship for vulnerable households.

Even if political reality requires phasing, the underlying principle remains: over time, the system should move toward capturing all unimproved land rent. When done responsibly, it reduces future rent-seeking while maintaining productive incentives.

There is also an important distributional effect: because a land value tax is ultimately borne by those who benefit from land location rent, it can reduce the extreme accumulation of wealth based purely on ownership of scarce land. When implemented broadly and transparently, it becomes a public mechanism for turning “private monopoly of location” into “public revenue for social use.”

6. What public benefit means: returning captured rent to society

A Georgist reform is not just about raising revenue. It is about transforming the purpose of taxation. When government captures land rent, that revenue can finance:

  • public goods that markets underprovide (infrastructure, safety, sanitation),
  • basic services and social stability,
  • education and civic investment,
  • and, in some proposals, redistribution through direct dividends.
